subtopic: ORGANIZATIONS FOR RELIEF OF DISTRESS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, many persons desire to assist in helping those who have suffered hardship and loss in the disastrous fires at Rimouski and Cabano, Quebec, and in the flooded areas of Manitoba. Yesterday, Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Peterborough West (Mr. Fraser) asked me a question to which I replied in part. I should now like to supplement the answer given.
As it is, of course, entitled to do, the United States government is establishing air defence zones in the eastern and the Pacific regions within its boundaries and therefore wants to be sure of the identity of aircraft entering those zones. The task of identification is greatly simplified if all aircraft entering the zones file flight plans, as the R.C.A.F., Canadian and United States air lines and many non-scheduled and private operators have been doing regularly for a long time.
In this connection, the civil aeronautics administration recently consulted the Canadian Department of Transport regarding the desirability of encouraging airmen to file flight plans prior to southbound flights across the international boundary between the 87th meridian in lake Michigan and the Atlantic coast, and between the 115th meridian a little west of Edmonton and the Pacific coast. As a result, on May 2, the Department of Transport issued a request to airmen, effective on May 5, to file flight plans prior to southbound flights across the boundary between the points mentioned. I understand that the United States authorities took similar steps at that time.
One of the main purposes of these notices was to take care of non-scheduled United States operators who constitute the bulk of the non-scheduled and private traffic crossing the boundary southbound. As I have indicated, the notices will not affect normal practice except as regards comparatively few non-scheduled and private operators, who will now be expected to file flight plans regularly for flights into the areas affected.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXCLUDE CERTAIN AREAS, ETC.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Gardiner (Minister of Agriculture) moved
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXCLUDE CERTAIN AREAS, ETC.
speechtext:
that the house go into committee to consider the following resolution:
That it is expedient to bring in a measure to amend the Prairie Farm Assistance Act. 1939, to exclude certain areas of land from the operation of the act; to repeal the limitation that the shape of blocks of sections brought into payment in ineligible townships should be rectangular in shape; and to provide further for the exemption from payment of the one per centum tax previously collected from certain flour mills.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXCLUDE CERTAIN AREAS, ETC.
speechtext: Is the minister not going to make a statement?

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXCLUDE CERTAIN AREAS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there _ is not much of a statement required in addition to what is in the resolution itself. It states clearly what the intention of the amendment is.
As all hon. members know, the Prairie Farm Assistance Act was first put on the statute book in 1939. The purpose of the act is to provide assistance to those who happen to live in what turns out to be a drought area. The method of determining whether it is a drought area or not is to check the crops in that particular area, and if the wheat crop is an average of eight bushels or less per acre, then certain payments are made. I would

like once again to say that the payments are not made on wheat. They are simply made on the farm operations in that area, whatever they may be. Wheat is used only as a means of determining whether payments should be made.
We have been functioning under that act from 1939 down to the present, and considerable money has been paid out to those farmers. We have amended the act from time to time, and on this occasion we are making three simple but fairly important amendments to the act. The purpose of the first one is to avoid making payments where we think they should not be made. That is, our intention under this act is to assist people who of necessity must remain for a time in what might be called submarginal areas, but our hope is eventually to get them off those lands. Therefore we have been organizing the submarginal lands into pastures under the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act.
In going over the areas this year in order to seek out new areas to organize into pastures, we did find that some persons were getting back on those submarginal lands oy obtaining what are known as cultivation leases. Under those cultivation leases they were operating, and of course if operating under the terms of the act as it now is they would collect. This bill proposes to make it impossible for persons to collect who have gone on lands that are owned by the federal government, a provincial government or a municipality, our view being that if either the federal government, a provincial government, or a municipal council lease lands to individual farmers for cultivation purposes, they should lease them on terms that will pay as well without any assistance under the Prairie Farm Assistance Act, as if they paid rent and obtained assistance. For that reason we are suggesting that payments should not be made on government owned lands.
We are making provision for the fact that there will be lands in those areas that to all intents and purposes are owned by the government through the Veterans Land Act. It is provided in the legislation that this exemption shall not apply to lands held under the Veterans Land Act. In other words, the payments will still be made there.
The next part of the bill does something which most members thought a year ago should have been done when this legislation was before the house. We then changed the unit that could be treated under the act so that it would be regarded as though it were an entire township, whether it was being dealt with because that particular area had more than ten bushels to the acre-in
Prairie Farm Assistance Act which case it went out-or whether it had less than eight bushels per acre, in which case it was brought in.
In the previous legislation we said it required nine sections or a quarter of a township to make it possible to bring areas in. Last year we amended that to say that it had to be only six sections, but we still continued the provision that it had to be rectangular. Under this amendment, whether an area is going in or coming out, under the terms of the payment the area may be six or more sections, and it does not require to be rectangular. It can be L-shaped, or T-shaped, or it can be some other shape, but it does not require to be rectangular.
The third part of the bill proposes to amend the section which provides for the collection of one per cent from all elevators and mills which operate in grain. This simply restricts the definitions of mills, so that it does not include all of what were termed "mills" two years ago. Prior to the war, all our larger mills were making flour from wheat for sale either in Canada or outside Canada, and the smaller mills were mostly engaged in the grinding of feed. During the war many of these smaller mills found it possible to make flour to sell to advantage, and did so. Under the act as it reads now, any grain delivered to these mills is taxed one per cent to assist in paying prairie farm assistance. Now the mills which have gone back to the milling of feed grains will not be taxed. In other words the tax will be confined to mills which are milling wheat which is to be sold into interprovincial and export trade, and perhaps also sold intraprovincially as well.
Those are the three amendments. I do not think there will be any great controversy about the need for putting them in the act. I suggest that since we are going to proceed with the discussion of the estimates there would be no necessity for discussing at this time details of payments, and so forth, because these matters can be discussed when the estimates are before the committee of supply.
I should like to say, however, that a very considerable number of members are not here this afternoon, because of a trip which was arranged and in which many of our members are taking part. I was asked by some of ithem, including the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) to assure them that we would not go beyond the stage of first reading this afternoon. I had hoped that we might have the resolution adopted and the bill presented. I have given the understanding that I will not suggest to the house that the measure go any further today, thus giving

Prairie Farm Assistance Act hon. members who are now absent, but who will be here at the beginning of the week, an opportunity to discuss it.

speechtext: Will the minister send the bill to the committee on agriculture, as has been done in the past?

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXCLUDE CERTAIN AREAS, ETC.
speechtext: I did not think there was anything in the bill sufficiently controversial to make that necessary.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXCLUDE CERTAIN AREAS, ETC.
speechtext: I am of course very much in favour of the first suggestion made by the minister. But with respect to the other two, may I ask, for purposes of clarification if for nothing else, whether those six sections must necessarily be together?

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXCLUDE CERTAIN AREAS, ETC.
speechtext: They must be together.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXCLUDE CERTAIN AREAS, ETC.
speechtext: They must be contiguous?

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXCLUDE CERTAIN AREAS, ETC.
speechtext: Yes, they must be contiguous, and must lie alongside a township already in.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXCLUDE CERTAIN AREAS, ETC.
speechtext:
I followed that; but there is no arrangement about shape

or is there some discretion in that matter?

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXCLUDE CERTAIN AREAS, ETC.
speechtext: I think the hon. member for Calgary West, knowing western Canada as well as he does, will understand me when I say that if you have six sections just one mile wide and six miles long lying alongside a township already in, they can come in, and there is no question about it. That is rectangular. If you have them two deep and three across, they can come in because they are rectangular. You could have three running north and south and two across, and they could still come in. But, under the act as it now stands, if you had four lying alongside an area already in, and then two on top of that, it would be impossible for them to get in. So that you could have zigzagging to the extent that there would be one section dropped out, and still you would have six. Or perhaps there would be two sections dropped out, and you would still have six-or you could have five in a block, and one on top of it. But it would have to be a continuous block of land. You could not take five at the bottom and put in one away up at the top to make the six.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXCLUDE CERTAIN AREAS, ETC.
speechtext: You could put six clear across?

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXCLUDE CERTAIN AREAS, ETC.
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXCLUDE CERTAIN AREAS, ETC.
speechtext: Would it not be better if the house were to go into committee so that these questions might be asked?

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXCLUDE CERTAIN AREAS, ETC.
speechtext: Before going into committee I should like to speak briefly.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXCLUDE CERTAIN AREAS, ETC.
speechtext:
I have only one question, and if it is answered I shall be


satisfied. In connection with these mills, did I understand the minister to say that a number of mills have gone back into the milling of feeds and out of the milling of flour?	.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXCLUDE CERTAIN AREAS, ETC.
speechtext: That is so. If it has not already developed in connection with some mills, it is expected that it will develop as we go along. For the purposes of this section, a mill now, in order to be taxable, must be one that has been declared by the parliament of Canada to be a work for the general advantage of Canada. If it is so declared, it is in the same position as an elevator.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXCLUDE CERTAIN AREAS, ETC.
speechtext: I understand.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXCLUDE CERTAIN AREAS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the house will welcome that feature of the resolution which removes the rectangular (provision covering six sections or larger blocks of land, which now can be joined to an eligible township. I am not just certain what is covered by the first part, which excludes certain areas of land from the operation of the act; ibu-t if I understood the minister correctly it would prevent people from going back on the P.F.R.A. pastures which contained submarginal lands, working that land and then becoming eligible for bonus. I certainly do not like to see at any time prairie farm assistance paid on submarginal lands; but I hope that this provision will not be used to prevent farmers, even though they have farmed on submarginal lands, from receiving payments as they have received them in the past.
I approve the removal of the rectangular provision from the six-section block. Since I was first elected to parliament in 1945, on every occasion I have brought to the attention of the minister the injustice that has arisen from adding only rectangular blocks. Crop failures in western Canada so often occur because of the way in which the showers happen to fall. They certainly do not fall in rectangles. I do not know whether they fall in L-shaped or T-shaped patterns, but certainly the T-shaped and L-shaped blocks would give more farmers the benefit of crop failure payments than the rectangular provision which is now applied.
I hope the minister will have this bill referred to the agriculture committee. In the past we have obtained real co-operation in that committee and have been given a good deal of information. Based on my experience I feel that the government has paid some attention to the proceedings of that committee, and as a result improvements in the act have been made from time to time. I repeat that I hope the minister will find it possible to send this bill to

that committee. It took only two or three hours of the time of the committee last year, and as the committee has not met so far this year it certainly would not be a burden on its members to consider this bill in greater detail.
There is another discrimination under the act which this resolution does not seek to relieve. I refer to the taking out of certain blocks of land. As the act now stands, a six-section block may be removed from an eligible township if the yield is more than ten bushels an acre. As always happens, there are farmers who have complete crop failures under the provisions of the act, that is, a yield of less than eight bushels per acre. As long as the rectangular provision is maintained when taking out certain blocks of land you are going to take out a number of farmers who in fact have crop failures.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXCLUDE CERTAIN AREAS, ETC.
speechtext: Perhaps I did not make myself clear. This applies to both.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXCLUDE CERTAIN AREAS, ETC.
speechtext:
I am glad it does. That is one more point in the minister's favour, and I hope he will keep on making others as I go along.
On March 23, 1950, as reported on page 1039 of Hansard, I asked the Minister of Agriculture if consideration would be given, in the amendments to be presented this session, to making the half-township unit apply to all sections of the act. The minister replied as follows:
We brought in an amendment last year which to all intents and purposes does that.
I have received a number of representations from farmers living in half townships where the yield has been less than four bushels to the acre, but who were not able to qualify under the act as it is now constituted. When an area is established as a crop failure area, if the department can find half a township outside of that area, perhaps in another province, perhaps a thousand miles away, then the people in the half township can obtain a payment based on the average crop yield in the half township. As I say, a number of instances were brought to my attention last fall in which a township had become eligible for the $1.50 per acre payment-the average yield in the township was between four and eight bushels per acre-but within that township there was a large area a half township or more in which the yield was less than four bushels to the acre. Those farmers could not obtain the $2.50 per acre payment because the average was based on the whole township.
I might demonstrate what I am trying to point out by referring to a specific case that was brought to my attention. I could give the 55946-154
Prairie Farm Assistance Act legal description of the township, but I do not think it is necessary for my purposes. The average yield was slightly over four bushels per acre. As a matter of fact for all the farmers within the township the yield exceeding four bushels per acre amounted to only 288 bushels, according to information from the farmers concerned. That meant that because a farmer had one-fifteenth of a bushel per acre more than the four bushels, he was denied assistance to the extent of $1 per acre. It amounted to about ten bushels of wheat for each farmer. Each farmer had ten bushels too much and was thus prevented from getting the larger payment. In other words, because the farmers in that township had $15 worth of wheat more than they should have had, they could not get the larger payment, and were thus denied payments up to $200 in the form of prairie farm assistance.
The north half of this township had almost a complete failure. The south half had somewhat better crops, but the yield was still under 8 bushels per acre. The average for the two halves meant that no one in the township was able to qualify for the $2.50 payment. I would hope that the half-township provision which is now applied in certain areas as long as they are removed from the crop failure area will be made the basis of payment under the act.
There is no doubt that the Prairie Farm Assistance Act has been of real benefit over the years to western Canada, particularly to that part of it which comprises the high risk crop area. While the act has been of real benefit in many respects, it is becoming less beneficial with each succeeding year. The payments under the act have remained the same since 1939, while during that ten year period the costs of farm production have practically doubled. It is true the one per cent deduction has remained the same, but because of the much better price of wheat and other grains at the present time the government can expect to get almost three times as much revenue with this one per cent deduction.
The largest amount that any farmer can receive in the form of prairie farm assistance is $500. Where a man is farming 400 acres of land, $500 is just a drop in the bucket. It would not even pay his seeding operations, much less the varied farm costs and the farmer's own cost of living. I should like to see the payments under the act increased. On the basis of present farm costs they should be increased to at least $5 or $6 per acre.
The Saskatchewan wheat pool organization, at their convention last fall, supported an increase in prairie farm assistance, though

Prairie Farm Assistance Act half or more of the delegates came from areas where there were not crop failures last year, and where crop failures are not usually experienced. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, while I welcome some features of the resolution, I should like to see the amount of payment increased.
I hope also that the time will come when areas added to an eligible township may be added on the basis of a section of land. While the rectangular provision is being removed, apparently the area cannot follow a zigzag pattern if the crop failure which occurs follows such a pattern. I hope that the half township may be made the unit throughout the act, in order to remove the discrimination that exists in the present legislation between persons living within a crop failure area and those living in a halftownship outside the crop failure area.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXCLUDE CERTAIN AREAS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is not my intention to take much time in discussing the resolution now before the house. The matter has been considered at considerable length, both in the house and in the standing committee on agriculture, since the act was first passed in 1939. The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) might have saved himself a lot of time and difficulty in the house if he had accepted many of the suggestions made from time to time in earlier years as to the operation of the legislation. I am glad to see that little by little he is accepting the views of many of his own supporters as well as members of the opposition, by bringing the act into conformity with requests that have been made.
As to the first amendment proposed by the resolution, I think we should wait until we have more information from the bill or otherwise before saying very much about it. We are in complete accord with the second part of the resolution, with the exception that we would like the minister to go a little further. He is learning to walk little by little, and if he could just take one more step it would be helpful. If he is not satisfied to bring it down to an individual basis, then let him bring it down to a section basis. Even during the past year we have had many complaints from farmers, who have had crops that were next to a failure, because they have been put into an area with farmers who had a good yield, and were thus denied the benefits of the Prairie Farm Assistance Act. I feel that is not the intention of the act, and if it were brought down to a section basis many of those in difficult financial circumstances would be able to receive the benefits of the legislation.
As to the third proposal suggested by the resolution, I do not feel that we have any complaint against it. Perhaps it will remove

some of the complaints of eastern farmers about the high price of feed. If it does not have the desired effect, I suggest that the profits of the dealers should be investigated because I feel that there lies most of the trouble as to the high prices that the eastern farmer has to pay. Western producers cannot be expected to take lower prices than they are accepting at the present time, particularly in view of the sacrifices they made during the war and for many years prior thereto. When the measure goes into committee we may have further questions to ask in order to get definite information, particularly about the first suggested amendment.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. Beaudoin in the chair.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXCLUDE CERTAIN AREAS, ETC.
speechtext:
I should like to ask the minister a question about the first part of the resolution, which reads:
That it is expedient to bring in a measure to amend the Prairie Farm Assistance Act, 1939, to exclude certain areas of land from the operation of the act.
I understood the minister to say that this applies only to lands which have now been declared community pastures.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXCLUDE CERTAIN AREAS, ETC.
speechtext: No.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXCLUDE CERTAIN AREAS, ETC.
speechtext: If it does not apply only to community pastures, then does it apply to provincial lands sold under a thirty-three year lease? In Saskatchewan school lands are being sold to individuals under a thirty-three year lease. I believe some of the farmers' co-operatives hold their land under a thirty-three year lease. Would the amendment to the act exclude those lands from payment under the Prairie Farm Assistance Act?

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXCLUDE CERTAIN AREAS, ETC.
speechtext:
It will exclude lands to
which title is held by governments, whether they be federal, provincial or municipal. If land is sold to someone under an agreement of sale, I presume he will hold it in the same way as any person holds land under such an agreement; but if it is land to which the clear title is held by the government, and not by anyone else, payment will not be made. Our argument is that when the government leases it, no matter under what kind of lease, it must be responsible for seeing that the individual gets the land on a lease under which he can make a go of it. If it is the federal government, then we should not take money out of the tax payments of the people of Canada to help to pay rent on land that an individual is working. The same thing should be true with regard to a province or a municipality. If the land is not worth anything, there should not be any rent for it. If it is worth only fifty cents an acre, the rent should not be more than fifty cents an

acre. We should not put people on land that is not worth anything, or is not worth the rent being charged for it, and then expect the taxpayers of Canada to help to pay the rent.
That is the general plan. It does not apply to the lands referred to a few moments ago by the hon. member for Assiniboia and by the hon. member for Melfort-lands that have already been taken into community pastures. It is presumed that individuals will not be able to go back on those lands. For example, we own the lands we have in community pastures in Saskatchewan, and we own them for the purpose of seeing to it that an individual does not get back on them. Once we put a fence around the pasture there is no difficulty about those lands. On the other hand, if we go to Saskatchewan, Alberta or Manitoba looking for lands to be put into community pastures, we may find that one or other of those governments has leased these lands to an individual, and therefore they are not available. We may be able to get possession of surrounding land, but that particular area is not available because it has been leased. We maintain that if it is going to be leased under those circumstances, then whoever leases it, whether it be the federal, a provincial or a municipal government, they should make provision for the individual, and it should not be made out of this fund.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXCLUDE CERTAIN AREAS, ETC.
speechtext: Do I understand the minister to say that all land in the special areas of Alberta which is under cultivation lease will not be eligible now for payment of the bonus? The minister knows that in Alberta land is divided into two classes. Land that is considered unsuitable for cultivation is leased on a grazing lease, and it cannot be cultivated. Land that is considered suitable for cultivation is leased for a period of twenty years under a cultivation lease. Do I understand the minister to say now that all that land cannot be eligible under this act? If so, it is going to affect adversely a great many farmers.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXCLUDE CERTAIN AREAS, ETC.
speechtext:
I understand it is perhaps two thousand quarter-sections, which is a considerable area of land scattered here and there, some of it in blocks; but if we permit that to go on I am afraid we shall not have a Prairie Farm Assistance Act at all in a very short time. Within the last few months we have found that as many as thirty-six quarters within one township have been leased in the areas where we are of opinion pastures should be formed. If that sort of thing is permitted to go on, I am quite sure the taxpayers in other parts of Canada are going to take very strong exception to it.
Prairie Farm, Assistance Act
For example, we find this in certain areas- and I do not want to go into too many details, because in doing so I may tread on somebody's toes. We find cases in which individual farmers are unable to collect on more than one 400-acre area; but by leasing a piece of land alongside through some member of the family the amount can be doubled,., or if two members of the family lease land it can be trebled. It was in checking lands in connection with that sort of thing that the difficulties were discovered, and of course that cannot be permitted to continue if we intend to keep this legislation in operation.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXCLUDE CERTAIN AREAS, ETC.
speechtext: The minister knows very well that originally that area was settled on a half-section basis. Over a period of time the farmers found they were not able to make a living on a half-section; many of them got into financial difficulties, and the land was offered for sale for taxes. The provincial government put up an initial bid; the mortgage companies claimed the land was not worth the amount asked, and let it go, which made it possible for the provincial government to lease back to the farmers areas of land considerably greater than a half-section. A half-section is not sufficient in that area to provide a living; so we find areas up to 2,000 and sometimes 3,000 acres being leased to individual farmers, and on that basis they are able to make a living. So far as cultivating land is concerned, the provincial government has made it a practice to grant cultivation leases only on land considered suitable for cultivation. The land is good; the only thing wrong with it is lack of moisture. In the initial stages those farmers were encouraged by the federal government of the time to go there and settle on a half-section basis. The government opened up the land and encouraged the people to go there. The people went there, and great sacrifices have been made in that area. The Prairie Farm Assistance Act was brought in to help out those farmers. Now I understand that under this legislation about eighty per cent of those farmers are to be declared ineligible for the bonus. Why, it is just going to cause a riot up there. The minister says the provincial government can pay, but he knows very well that is not the solution of the problem.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXCLUDE CERTAIN AREAS, ETC.
speechtext: May I ask what are the terms of those leases?

speechtext:

Prairie Farm Assistance Act and far cheaper than the rate of taxes in other areas, where they run to $70, $80 and $90 per quarter section. The amount they pay is considerably less than that.
The minister knows the solution-it is irrigation. The government has been talking irrigation ever since 1922. It is true that certain amounts of money have been voted during each of the past three years or so, and they are doing a certain amount of work now, but we are still a long way from getting that land irrigated under the Red river diversion project. So far the only thing the government has done, apart from making surveys, has been to put up small dams to create reservoirs from the run-off water. Unfortunately, however, in very dry years there is no run-off water, and just at the time we need the water most for irrigation it is not available. Now the minister is just going to get out of the whole thing by declaring that no bonus will be paid on land under lease from the government, though all the land in that area is under lease with the exception of the odd section here and there which is privately owned. The minister is now asking us to support the proposal that this whole area in Alberta shall be declared ineligible under this act unless it is privately owned, and I do not think he can present one argument to show that this is fair.

those payments for the other half they have leased? In other words, though only half that township is privately owned, if there is a crop failure throughout the township so that the total amount of cultivated land produced less than four bushels to the acre, will those people get the assistance for the half of the land which they own?

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXCLUDE CERTAIN AREAS, ETC.
speechtext:
They will get assistance on the basis of the land they own, which means they can be paid on half their cultivated acreage up to 400 acres. If a man is cultivating 800 acres it does not matter where it is, whether it is in that area or anywhere else; he is paid only on 200 acres, and that would continue to be the case with land owned in any part of the entire area. If he had land elsewhere, outside that area, it would not come into the picture. The sort of area that creates trouble for us, and which I am sure every hon. member would agree should not come in, is where you have an area that has been declared submarginal, or if it has not been declared so at least we have paid prairie farm assistance for every year but one of the eleven years we have been giving that assistance, which very definitely shows that people cannot farm in that area. Some of it is land which in the thirties, prior to the war, had been allowed to go back; the people left it, in some cases, and it remained uncultivated. In other areas the individuals who purchased the land simply dropped it and let the payments go, so they do not own it now and finally it has reverted to the government. A farmer and his son may live on a section alongside land of that kind. The farmer may have 400 acres broken, so we would pay him on 200 acres. Then the son gets a cropping lease on the next half section, and he has another two or three hundred acres broken there. By breaking that land you -can bring in all that block. You can get it in two 400-acre blocks, and cause P.F.A.A. to pay on all of it. We find we have been doing that; and if we go on doing that year after year, and -those cases keep multiplying, I can imagine what will happen eventually, and what would have happened if the opposition had found it out first. I was pleased that I found it out last summer when we were looking for areas to put pastures in; because I know what would happen to this government if we let it get out in the public accounts committee as something which was raised by someone else that we pay out thousands of dollars, -and maybe it might run into hundreds of thousands of dollars on payments of that kind. We paid out $20 million last year. If we pay a considerable part of it out of the treasury on submarginal lands that are owned

by the government, whether it be this government, the Alberta government, the Saskatchewan government, the Manitoba government or one of the municipal governments, I am quite sure that before we got through with the discussion, if we had not blown the act up, we would have come close to it.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXCLUDE CERTAIN AREAS, ETC.
speechtext: As I understand the minister, it is not a case of changing the act now so that payment will be made only on land that is not submarginal. If the minister wants to change the act so that payments are made only on land suitable for grain and if at the same time he will do something else under the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act to rehabilitate these people who have been taken off submarginal land for wheat production, that is O.K. But what the minister is suggesting now, as I understand it, is not that they are going to remove submarginal land entirely from the application of the Prairie Farm Assistance Act, but that the government is going to remove entirely land owned by the provincial government or other governments and leased to farmers within the various provinces. I think that kind of policy of the government is most discriminatory. I do not think this government should be attempting to dictate to the government of Alberta or to the government of Saskatchewan by what method they should dispose of provincial land. Over the last few years in Saskatchewan we have leased a great many parcels of land to young veterans on the basis of a 33-year lease. speechtext: I will send my hon. friend over a copy of the bill, and he will be able to discuss it to better advantage.

speechtext: I appreciate that. But I certainly have the strongest possible objection to what the minister has already told us.

speechtext: I do not think there is anybody who objects to land which consistently has had to have P.F.A. paid on it being withdrawn and having something else done with it; either put it into community pastures or put it back into grass and move the people who are on it onto land where they can make a decent living without having to receive the P.F.A.A. bonus from year to year. speechtext: No.

In the northern part of the province there is a good deal of school land which has been held under a 33-year lease from the provincial government. Occasionally we get a crop failure there; it is only once in every ten years, but we pay one per cent every year. Now you say that these lands, because they are held under a 33-year lease, or a 20-year lease, or whatever the lease may be, from the provincial government, are not entitled to payment. should exclude the grain that is grown on this land from the one per cent levy, because otherwise he is puting a tax in perpetuity on the grain that is grown on that land and is saying to the people who are growing the grain, "You can never get a payment under the P.F.A.A."

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXCLUDE CERTAIN AREAS, ETC.
speechtext: There are other lands in Canada that are submarginal besides those in Alberta or in the western provinces. Under the present set-up they never hope to get anything but they always have to pay something, as I understand it. But if we were going to go on spending more money each year, as remarked by the minister some time ago, the people were going to object to these payments in time and they would find out that some of us were paying too much for this type of legislation. In fact, as I understand it, the two acts are working one against the other. One is trying to build up an area and the other is trying to keep people on land when they should be somewhere else. I think I should give the year by year payments in round figures rather than read them all over. In the first year it was $10 million; in the second year $6,750,000. The first year was 1939.

These are payments. In
1941,	the third year, the payments were $15,500,000. There was nothing at all in
1942,	although the collection went right on that year. In 1943, $7,500,000; in 1944, almost $6 million; in 1945, almost $17 million; in 1946, $10,800,000; in 1947, $17 million; in 1948, $14 million; in 1949, $20 million, a total of $124,749,758.15.
I might indicate how the collections run. In the first years, of course, the price of grain

was low, and while the total amount of grain marketed was much similar to what is still being marketed, the amount collected was much lower because it is one per cent that is collected and not so much a bushel. In the first year the amount collected was about $2,500,000; in the second year it was about $2,500,000; the third year was a very poor year, and about $1,500,000 was collected. In the year 1942, $2,700,000 was collected and in 1943-44, when the prices got higher, $4,700,000 was collected. In the next year, $5,300,000; in the next year, $3,400,000; in the next year, $5,100,000; in the next year $5,100,000 and in 1948-49, $6,600,000. In 1949-50, the year we are now in, it has amounted to $5,350,000 up to the present, but we have not completed the crop year yet.

Why not
increase the payment of the one per cent? Why not increase it to three per cent and let the western provinces pay their own insurance? Why ask the rest of Canada to carry this?

speechtext: I believe I can answer that question very well and save the minister the trouble of doing it because it might be embarrassing to him. You are not excluded.
Prairie Farm Assistance Act

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXCLUDE CERTAIN AREAS, ETC.
speechtext:
We are excluded in a sense. I had this all out with an area down at Gladstone, in Manitoba, the first year that we had the bill. I was invited there by the people of the area and they had the reeve of the municipality in the chair. They had the hall packed, and I was not supposed to have been able to get out of there with a whole hide when the meeting was over. I went and met the farmers there and I said to them: On the estimate that we made when we put the bill through this house we said that there would be about $3 over a long period, say twenty or more years, taken out of the treasury for every $1 that is paid into this fund. The house accepted that; and in answer to my hon. friend who spoke a moment ago, all the issues which he suggested a moment ago were then brought up in the house and threshed out; and finally it was unanimously accepted. I think I am right in saying that we finally got the amending bills associated with this matter through the house almost unanimously on every occasion.
What I said to those people then is what I say today. I said to them:	"You tell me
that because you have never had a crop failure, and you never will have one, you should not pay anything into this." I said: "If I have got to admit that, I have got to go back to the house and say that the people in Montreal and Toronto who never will have a crop, let alone a crop failure, should not be asked to pay into this." I said: "I do not know of any way that you can set up crop failure insurance in western Canada that could be carried on a basis of charging it up to the land itself." I do not know of any system under which it could be done.
Since, we have proven that it could be done in Manitoba. We have proven that it might be done in about one-third of Alberta. It could not be done over the whole province of Alberta; and we have certainly proven that there would be no possibility of doing it at all over the province of Saskatchewan.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXCLUDE CERTAIN AREAS, ETC.
speechtext: It could up in northeastern Saskatchewan.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXCLUDE CERTAIN AREAS, ETC.
speechtext:
Still the province of Saskatchewan produces half of all the wheat that is produced in Canada, and wheat itself provides, if not the greatest, the second greatest medium from which we obtain new wealth year by year in the country; and it certainly provides the greatest tonnage of exports, with one possible exception, that is shipped out of this country to bring into the country new dollars or new wealth of one kind or another.
We argued at that time, and we still argue, that on that basis everyone in Canada has some justification for believing that it is a

Prairie Farm Assistance Act good thing to keep that country operating, and to give it a sufficient amount of insurance to carry along; but I do not know of any arrangement under which we could do it and argue that the farmer who is never going to have a loss in western Canada should not pay anything and the other fellow should attempt to pay it all; or even any basis upon which you can say that the farmers who are never going to have a loss should pay sufficient in in order to take care of the other group that are ' operating in the interests of all Canada. We have been able to maintain this legislation on a co-operative basis. I had hoped we would not get into a discussion of that general question. We have discussed it before; we have threshed it out; we have finally come to the conclusion-that is those of us who were here at the time. I am sure the same thing would happen all over again if we discussed it long enough-that this is one of the best pieces of legislation that we have in the country from the standpoint of all the people of Canada.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXCLUDE CERTAIN AREAS, ETC.
speechtext: Don't spoil it.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXCLUDE CERTAIN AREAS, ETC.
speechtext:
The reason we do not want to do things that are unreasonable, that other people cannot accept, is that that would spoil it.
I am quite prepared to argue here in the house, or anywhere out in the country in the area that is concerned, or anywhere else, that to deliberately go on year after year making payments to make it possible for people, without investing any capital in it at all, to get onto submarginal lands in western Canada, which ought to be in pasture, and try to farm them is wrong.
I am prepared to go anywhere and argue that payment under this act should not be made in such cases. Then, coming back to the questions asked, it has been suggested by most of the members who have spoken critically of it that if this was going to result in lands that are to be in pasture remaining in pasture, and lands which are submarginal being in pasture, and the private lands outside being in a position to be farmed, they would then be prepared to consider the matter more or less favourably.
Now the present position, as it has been stated by the hon. member for Middlesex East-and he has stated it correctly-is that we have been told in the house, I have told it to the house on many occasions, that we have two acts, one of which is the Prairie Farm Assistance Act, and the other P.F.R.A.
Under P.F.R.A. we offer to take any lands that are submarginal, put a fence around them, regrass them, put water in them and then allow the farmers who are located round about to organize themselves into pasture areas and put their cattle up to the number


of two-thirds of all that that area will accommodate into those pastures from year to year at a small fee. We have a million and a quarter acres of that land organized today on that basis. This government has purchased the lands that had to be purchased, and paid for them. They have assisted people to move off those lands and to go somewhere else. They have helped those people to get lands, and resettle themselves somewhere else. We have gone on to say that we are prepared to do that in Manitoba, prepared to do it in Saskatchewan and prepared to do it in Alberta. Now, so far, we have not got any lands in Alberta under that plan.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXCLUDE CERTAIN AREAS, ETC.
speechtext: The provincial government have leases.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXCLUDE CERTAIN AREAS, ETC.
speechtext: If they wish to run some show of their own, then I have no objection to their doing it. But I hope they will not expect the taxpayers of Canada to pay for a plan which has not been worked out here and agreed to in the House of Commons.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXCLUDE CERTAIN AREAS, ETC.
speechtext: That has nothing to do with the cultivation lease.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXCLUDE CERTAIN AREAS, ETC.
speechtext:
It is a very simple matter for the government of the province of Alberta to organize those areas so as to bring them under the act, even as we are proposing to draft it today. But I do not think they should ask the government of Canada in Ottawa or ask this House of Commons to do for them what it is not necessary to do in order to have the matter dealt with as they want it dealt with.
I agree that there are lands all through the constituency my hon. friend represents-I have driven over practically all of them- which should never be farmed, as the hon. member knows. And I know he would never be a party to saying that they should be. Then there are other lands there which are very good, and ought to be irrigated. And both the provincial and the federal governments are working toward that end. Then there are lands in that area owned and operated by private individuals. They have been living there a long time, and by getting a sufficient area around under lease from the government or from somewhere else to be used for pasture, they can live there, and live just about as well as they could live anywhere else.
But I do not think any of us are worrying very much about what the proposed bill is doing'to those people. We certainly do not want to do them an injustice. But we do want to put this legislation in shape whereby no one can come into this House of Commons

and say, "You are paying money out on submarginal lands which are owned by a government and should be under pasture", this government is prepared to put it under pasture for the common good and someone deliberately goes on it and gets a lease, and makes it impossible to do that. I do not think the House of Commons wants us to pay to continue that.
I think there might be some good in the suggestion made by the hon. member for Assiniboia at the beginning of his remarks. There is just the possibility that out of the discussion which might take place in committee some who are now afraid of this legislation might be convinced that it is all right. There is just the possibility that some also may be able to bring forward some suggestions which would result in allaying to some extent the fears now held by some hon. members.
But I hope that nothing will come out of committee which will make it possible for anyone to continue going around and picking off pieces of land which they can get on leases, and into which they can put $100 or $200 or $300, and then pull out of this government $200 to $500 to make it possible for them to live there for a year. I hope that will not be permitted by anything that is done in committee or in the house. However, I am quite prepared to see that when the bill receives second reading we send it to committee so that we may have it threshed out in committee, so that we may know what the facts are, and then have our legislation go through with everyone understanding what is meant.

speechtext:
I agree with the minister that the bill under the circumstances should go to the committee on agriculture. However, I should like to clear up one point. There was one question which, by the way, he did not answer, although he spoke for thirty minutes. I did not say anything about the one per cent levy being paid in my constituency and in his own area by people who never hope to obtain anything out of the act. But now he is excluding lands in the southern part of the province where there will be crop failures, and where they will not have the money to pay the one per cent levy, 55946-155
Prairie Farm Assistance Act as we have in the north, where we are fortunate enough to grow good crops. However, I do not wish to prolong the discussion now. That can be discussed in committee.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXCLUDE CERTAIN AREAS, ETC.
speechtext: I shall answer the question. I do not think we should be agreeing to any lands in your district or in my district or any other district being under this act where the land itself will not show as much as one per cent earnings. And the suggestion is made that there are some of these lands on which they are paying up to one-ninth or one-eighth of the crop into the provincial government. It could be into this government or some other government. Well, one-eighth is not much and one-ninth is not much. But on some farms that would get close to being the $200 or $500 in some cases that can be paid out under this act. With the exception of what I have suggested, I do not know what the particular means should be, but certainly from the point of view of long-range conservation measures there is no doubt we are still cultivating far too much land in the dry areas of Saskatchewan and Alberta.
As a boy I was raised on a ranch in southern Saskatchewan. It was beautiful ranching country, and it was opened up for homesteading. We then moved to Alberta. I have only been back once, in 1931, and I did not recognize the area. It was just a desert. There was a nice creek flowing

Prairie Farm Assistance Act through the place that always had water in it, and you could not tell where the 'course of it had been. It had been completely filled in. He will also have to buy a full line of equipment. Therefore he is most happy if he can get a half section of land from the provincial government under a leasing arrangement. That was done long before. As a matter of fact the picture my hon. friend has in mind and that I have in mind began to be formed back in 1922. I believe it was commenced at least that far back. It was not under any of the gentlemen who have been mentioned when it was started, but it has gradually developed to the present position. It is only necessary to drive over that area to understand why that action was taken. When it comes to the other matter, however, knowing that both provincial governments had legislation on their statute books empowering them to declare any area submarginal and to commence to move people out of it, we put that provision in our statute. That was their own intention; those acts have been on the statute books of the provinces for a long time. So in this act we said that any land declared submarginal under that provincial legislation would not receive prairie farm assistance.
Then we set up the P.F.R.A., under which we organized this large area I mentioned a few moments ago, about 110,000 acres, some of which was owned by the government and
2440	HOUSE OF
Prairie Farm Assistance Act some by individuals. We bought out the individuals, and the provincial government gave us back the leased land. We had turned it over to them for nothing in 1931, and they gave it back to us for nothing in 1939 or 1940. We organized it into pastures, and bought up other lands to put in with it. Then we irrigated lands alongside it, in the Frenchman river valley, and people are living there and growing fodder, and stock is run in this large pasture. To any individual who wanted to live inside that fence we said, "You are on submarginal land, and you will get no prairie farm assistance." We have done that in every pasture we have set up, and those pastures now total some 1,300,000 acres in that area. To every person who wanted to remain there we said, "If you stay you remain under these conditions. In the first place, you have to get out through our fence. Then you have to put up with other people's cattle running around your place. In addition, you will not receive any prairie farm assistance; that is provided by our act."
Now we are going into other similar areas and saying we are prepared to put a fence around them and make pastures out of their land. There are perhaps only half a dozen or so people in the area, and we would like to have them move out. But now we find that svithin the last two or three years as many ,:as thirty-six people have moved into one Township in that area, and taken up crop leases. I do not think anyone in this house will suggest that we should continue to pay prairie farm assistance on that land. The situation is different in the case of a man who has been living on a piece of land for twenty or thirty years; who settled on that land years ago, when he did not know and no one knew what the conditions were. That man owns his land, or is living on it under an agreement of sale of some kind. He has managed to get along up to the present. We are not saying to him that unless he gets inside the pasture fence he must move off the land. We are saying, "Until we can find some place to put you we will help you along and pay the prairie farm assistance. Sooner or later, by obtaining this other land that still belongs to the province, to the municipality or to someone else, we hope to be able to get it organized into a pasture, and then we will help you move into an irrigated area, or somewhere else." In such cases we have undertaken to help a man take down his buildings; we have trucked them for him to his new location, and have helped pay the cost of putting them up again. So it is a matter of persuasion rather than compulsion, as my hon. friend suggested it might be. As long as we are going along with that policy we do not think we should turn around and


assist people to settle in these areas, by taking over cultivation leases, and getting prairie farm assistance. We do not think we should pay it.

Alberta and Saskatchewan had nothing to do with settlers coming in and settling on that land. .Alberta and Saskatchewan were not even yet born as provinces. They were territories in those days. What was to be done in order to assist these new provinces? What we are really debating today has a great deal to do with that very question. I do not think any hon. member, or anyone in the country, would say that because the dominion government had settled wide areas of that land with settlers, and put prospective provinces in the position in which they would have to pay crop failure relief, seed grain relief and a number of other things of that sort, and provide social services, schools and the like in areas that were not able to support such

We have now got to the point where what the minister seems to be arguing is this: If the dominion government is going to come into the province of Saskatchewan and take over this bad situation which has grown up during the years, then the dominion government requires that as a price of that assistance, that remedy, the province shall surrender to the dominion government the ownership of that land which properly belongs to Saskatchewan. The dominion government has created a situation in the province of Saskatchewan which is beyond the capacity of any province like Saskatchewan unaided to take care of financially or any other way. When it is discovered that the situation is beyond control and the dominion government comes in to discharge a responsibility which certainly morally they assumed when they put the settlers in the area, when the dominion government comes in to deal with the problem and assumes the responsibility, it says: You will have to give back the country to us.

1.	Departmental administration, $293,670.

There are a few questions I should like to ask on this item as it might be easier to ask them now rather than to wait until the various items they concern are before the committee. One matter has to do with the expenditures for miscellaneous, sundries, n.o.p.-not otherwise provided for -and contingent. Dealing with the Department of Agriculture alone they amount to a total of $198,159. Although it does not have to do with this department, I may say in passing that I have gone through all the estimates and I find the grand total for all departments is $17,382,354 for sundries, miscellaneous, not otherwise provided for, and in some cases contingent expenses. I believe that should be explained by the Minister of Finance if not by the Minister of Agriculture. If such expenses amount to so much then it would seem to me that they should be set out in greater detail or the departments should get together and agree on a common plan to deal with them.
The total for travelling expenses, for instance, in the Department of Agriculture for 1950-51 is $2,148,000, an increase of $171,500 over last year. I think the minister should answer these questions. I realize a great deal of travelling must be done by officials of the department but certainly not that much. In the case of sundries there is something else I should like to point out. It happens that thirteen out of the forty-five votes for sundry items are exactly the same as they were last year. They include such figures as $617, $513, $1,147, and they are identical with last year's items. I think that arouses a little suspicion and calls for an answer. Is the minister not going to answer?
I will wait until I hear more, if there is any more criticism. I want to look up these sundries.

I am not going to follow the criticism of the hon. member for Brant-Went-worth. Under this item I want to deal in a general way with an industry with which I am fairly familiar, fruit growing in the Okanagan valley. I should like to express my appreciation and that of the industry as a whole for the co-operation and assistance given to the industry by the Minister of Agriculture. I should like to point out, however, that if it were not for the disasters at Winnipeg and Rimouski you would probably be hearing a good deal more about the plight of the fruit growers of the Okanagan valley. While their disaster is not as great as those featured in the papers at the present time, they have received a terrible set-back through loss of markets and particularly because of the severe winter. I have heard from several of my friends in the industry saying that they have lost some of their orchards, peaches and apricots particularly. The value of their loss has not been completely assessed so I am not going to deal with that now. I should like to point out to the minister that I hope he has provision in his estimates to take care of the farmers who have suffered heavy losses.
I am also satisfied that the total amount of money received from all sales of apples up to date plus the $2 million generously given by the government will fall far short of returning to the farmers the cost of production. I hope if they come to the minister he will treat them in his usual co-operative way as he has in the past. I should like to review briefly the prospects for the coming year as it has a bearing on the situation of the fruit growers. I want to refer to the Penticton Herald of May 4. Mr. Embrey, an official of the British Columbia Tree Fruits Limited, is reported as saying that the estimate for the present year for apples is five and a half to six million boxes, which is roughly 70 per cent of last year's crop. He goes on to say that apricots and peaches will be practically nil. I do not think it is quite that bad but I am using his own words. He says that the cherry crop is expected to be about 30 per cent in comparison with last year's crop.
I merely point out that the fruit growers have suffered from loss of markets and conditions following a severe winter. They are battling natural obstacles plus artificial trade barriers. Mr. Embrey goes on to point out that the apple growers of Washington and other states, whose apples are in competition with our own over the border, are fighting hard to get Mr. Truman to place an import quota on Canadian apples. Nevertheless Mr. Supply-Agriculture
Embrey has hopes that will not be the case, and I think Mr. Truman has sympathetic feelings toward the Canadian growers. Our people are constantly in search of world markets, and I want to suggest some places where the government can help. One of them is by entering wholeheartedly into the principle of a world food pool. We feel that apples-and doctors have said so on many occasions-are needed as a part of any balanced diet. They are a necessity and should be used to balance the diet of every household the whole year round.
In the world as a whole there is a vast shortage of apples but in Canada, as is well known, we have a large surplus. I want to read a resolution passed by the growers at their convention last November concerning the suggestion I am endeavouring to pass on to the government. The resolution reads:
Whereas the food and agriculture organization has adopted in principle the world food pool resolution submitted by the Canadian Federation of Agriculture to and adopted by the international federation of agricultural producers at Guelph, Ontario, last June, which resolution conforms with submissions made by the British Columbia Federation of Agriculture during the last ten years, and
Whereas the FAO international commodity clearing house seeks to establish-
1.	''The maintenance of a high level of production and employment."
2.	"The reduction of trade restrictions, including tariffs and quantitative and monetary restrictions."
3.	"An increase in the standards of productive efficiency particularly in western Europe."
4.	"International investment to finance export and import surpluses" and
5.	"The restoration of convertible currencies and multi-lateral transactions as a basis of world trade" -all of which is designed to feed properly an undernourished world and thus utilize all presently available potential food and fibre production.
Therefore, the British Columbia Fruit Growers Association in its 1950 annual convention commends the Canadian Federation of Agriculture for promoting so effectively the world food pool principle and the sixty-one countries which make up FAO for planning to put this world-essential principle into active operation, and urges the Canadian government to give this project its complete support.
On their behalf, Mr. Chairman, I am passing on the desire and hope that the minister's support will be given to this resolution. Under those conditions we would have no surpluses. Instead of embarrassing us, they would be converted into tangible wealth. It would help build up good will throughout the world, and would put the industry on its feet. I believe our ability to produce is a sacred trust, and if we violate it or destroy our production by waste or dumping, some day we shall have to pay the price and answer for our actions.
Since Canada is one of the world's leading agricultural producers, Canadians should give leadership, and by that I mean we should

Supply-Agriculture
break all the economic red tape that is now tying us down to orthodox methods of trading with other countries. We shall be sorry indeed if the day ever comes when Canadian farmers, whether wheat growers or fruit producers, are asked to restrict their production. To me that is contrary to the laws of nature, and should not be done. In the light of that I ask the government to study the implications of this resolution, a copy of which was sent to the minister. My appeal is ably backed by Mr. Hannam, president of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture. He has summarized the matter in these words, and I quote from his statement in the Ottawa Journal of April 20:
"The problem, then, is largely a matter of distribution of food within each country and throughout the world. To have embarrassing surpluses of food piling up in one part of the country, undermining both producers' security and their domestic economies, while in some other parts of the world millions are hungry and undernourished, is a denial of everything that leads to human progress.
"Our farmers and farmers in other exporting countries will be compelled to restrict production against their better judgment if a world food plan is not undertaken to distribute abundance to people in great need. A continuation of this situation is a threat to the peace of the world, because you can't talk peace to hungry people nor can you argue successfully against communism, whcse leaders take full advantage of that kind of situation," concluded Mr. Hannam.
As I have stated already, I bring up this matter in the hope that the Minister of Agriculture, who is capable of taking the lead and who is in the happy position of having these surpluses more or less under control, can step into the picture and present the case to the rest of the world. I should like to compliment the minister and his department on what they have done, but I understand the difficulties they are up against, particularly with respect to foreign markets. When I came to investigate what were the actual handicaps I understood those difficulties better than ever. I find that one difficulty is the lack of peace treaties, [DOT] with which I shall deal later on. Recognition of countries which were formerly enemies, who are now in a position to deal with us, has not taken place owning to the absence of a peace treaty. Presumably that is a matter that will have to be dealt with by the Department of External Affairs. Then the Department of Finance comes into the picture of world trade, with our austerity program and the conservation of dollars. Into the same picture comes the Department of National Revenue, with its tariffs, quotas, duties and so on. So the Department of Agriculture has to make the best of a huge production and huge surplus, and battle against the interests of the other departments.

I suggest that the department exercise the powers granted in 1946, which to me appear very wide, in order to overcome some of the obstacles to which I have referred. The Canadian Commercial Corporation Act gives that corporation power to assist in the development of trade between Canada and other nations, and to assist persons in Canada to obtain goods and commodities from outside Canada or to dispose of goods and commodities that are available for export from Canada. Then in section 5 it provides:
. . . the corporation may carry on the business of:
(a)	importing goods or commodities into Canada, and
(b)	exporting goods or commodities from Canada, either as principal or as agent, in such manner and to such extent as it deems advisable to achieve the said purposes.
To my mind that gives the department power to work in conjunction with the corporation to set up an import-export board or its equivalent to take care of the marketing of our fruit products overseas. I realize it has been suggested that we have trade envoys to do these things; or, as one minister suggested, the industry itself should have representatives seeking these markets. The trouble is that a small firm, or any firm as far as that goes, finds it difficult to obtain properly qualified people to send abroad, mainly because of the cost involved. You need men able to speak the languages of the countries in which you are seeking to do business. They must be trained to ascertain the trade requirements of various countries, and so on. For many years we in Canada were indifferent to the trade needs of countries such as Britain, for instance. Their timber dimensions vary widely from ours, yet we stubbornly kept on sending our own dimensions. As a result it was many years before we realized why we were not making headway in that market. We also need a body that will have power to advise Canadian manufacturers and producers as to the requirements of these markets. These would include such things as timber dimensions, which I just mentioned, and the type, quality and size of pack with respect to fruit. We have probably drifted into world trade; we have gradually caught up with the trend, but we are still in the drift.
In the absence of any such policy, such bodies as the Canadian chamber of commerce are doing their best to overcome the difficulties. I should like to quote from a letter recently received from this organization to show what they are doing to fill the gap in the absence of a department organized to look after our import and export needs:
. . . anything which diminishes the output of our primary industries is bound to affect all business.

Primary industries, as you know, are dependent to a large extent upon foreign markets. Fluctuations in foreign trade can be related directly to your business. A continued deterioration of foreign trade could have the same damaging effect on primary industries in this province as weather adversity.
Regardless of whether we sell to the foreign market or not, we should be concerned about it. It seems obvious that we as individuals can do little. We can, however, support an organization which has as its objective the study and development of improved foreign trade.
You may have read in recent press dispatches of the return of Mr. Howard T. Mitchell of Vancouver from Anglo-Canadian trade talks in London, England. This is only one of the efforts of the Canadian chamber of commerce in this field. Undoubtedly such continued efforts will benefit British Columbia greatly.
Item stands.
