I should like to say another word, Mr. Chairman, on this bill before it gets out of committee. When I last spoke in the debate on the second reading of one of these bills-I think it was before the Easter recess-I said that I did not intend to take up any further time of the house in debating these measures. I spoke only briefly at that time.
When we were debating the bills on second reading, the chorus from the supporters of the bills was, "Let us get the bills through the house and to the appropriate standing committee where we can get all the information that our hearts can desire". Eventually the bills reached the committee, but once they got there the situation changed. Instead of making an attempt to get all the information required, the chorus began to get the bills back into the house. As I may mention later, that strategy had results which the strategists did not expect. Some members of the committee, and some who were not on the committee, but who were interested in the bills, were disgusted with what they saw and heard. The result was that they changed their minds, and their support for the bills
Prairie Transmission Lines is not nearly so strong now-at least not among the members from my province-as it was before the bills went to the committee.
On the order paper each Tuesday and Friday, and on private members days' on Mondays-I was going to say the perpetual private members' Mondays-these bills appear under the heading "private bills". In order to bring the heading of the bills in proper relation to reality, I think we should have a new page on the order paper, and put these bills under the title "privileged bills"; because I have never heard of a situation such as this one, where outside promoters can get greater preference in the House of Commons than can the members who were sent here by the electors of this country.
I think, however, that the long debate has had some good results. I notice that the hon. member for Vancouver South who, I am sorry to say, is not in his seat tonight, in an article written for a neighbourhood paper in his constituency said this:
The tragedy of the filibuster has been that it held parliament in contempt to the extent that it prevented members from exercising their responsibilities.
Then he went on to say something that we have heard time and time again during the debate on these bills and to which I shall refer later:
Parliament has no power to determine route of any pipe line but this authority is vested with the board of transport commissioners. Parliament has no authority to sanction either gas or oil for these pipe lines-this is the responsibility of the Alberta gas and oil conservation board. Export of these and like commodities is subject to statute of the Department of Trade and Commerce.
The filibuster, if the hon. member for Vancouver South wishes to call it that, has surely had at least one favourable result. It has held up discussion on these bills long enough for some of the British Columbia members, who were definitely in favour of the bills before they went to committee, to oppose them now in their present form at least while the others, with the possible exception of the one who is supporting the bills, do not know just where they stand.
To refer again to the hon. member for Vancouver South, in some remarks he made in the house in connection with the bills he said that he would vote for them and would go back to British Columbia and educate the people of that province into demanding an all-Canadian route. If there is need for education, it is the hon. member for Vancouver South that needs it. It is the people of British Columbia who are educating the hon. member for Vancouver South as they have educated the hon. member for Coast-Capilano, the hon. member for Comox-Alberni and quite
House of
Prairie Transmission Lines a number of other members who are at the moment sitting on the fence, not knowing which way they are going to fall.
The argument has been made and reiterated, that this parliament has no authority or power to designate a route. For my part, I would hate to believe that of this parliament. But whether or not parliament has the right to designate a definite route, surely parliament has a right to indicate what general route this House of Commons believes the pipe lines should follow in taking a Canadian natural resource from one point in Canada to another. Surely parliament has the right to say that. If not, we had better leave at once for our homes. The argument made by my hon. friends who are supporting these bills is that parliament need not do that. The board of transport commissioners will protect the interests of the people of Canada. Well, the board of transport commissioners have authority over our freight rates.

subtopic: FRAIRIE TRANSMISSION LINES LIMITED
speechtext: They have made mistakes before.

subtopic: FRAIRIE TRANSMISSION LINES LIMITED
speechtext:
My hon. friend says that they have made mistakes. A great many people in this parliament are not satisfied with the board of transport commissioners as they have dealt so far with freight rates. We have appointed a royal commission to look into freight rates because we are dissatisfied with the way the board of transport commissioners has been handling the job.
The board of transport commissioners was not sent to this house by the people of British Columbia to protect their interests. The people who were sent here to do that are the members from the constituencies in that province; and either we protect the interests of the people of British Columbia or we should stop making the alibi that that is the duty of the board of transport commissioners.
It is unnecessary to say a great deal on that point. When he spoke on this question a few evenings ago, the leader of the opposition made the point very clear, so clear, really, that there is no possibility of misunderstanding it. That is, that the first authority which must deal with the route the pipe line is to take is the government of Canada, and that the board of transport commissioners cannot and will not deal with the route until the government of Canada has made its decision in regard to it.
I read in a book once a saying that was attributed to the late Lord Randolph Churchill, father of Winston Churchill, to the effect that whenever you were in the position where you had to say a kind word about a political opponent in the House of Commons you should always be careful to do it with a


kick instead of a pat. 1 have never accepted that philosophy, and tonight I want to say a good word for the leader of the opposition. I believe hon. members and the people of Canada should be grateful to the leader of the opposition for the clear statement he made on this matter when he spoke in this debate on Tuesday evening last. Let me draw the committee's attention briefly to what he said. I shall not quote from his speech extensively, but only a small part of it. He read from a minute of council, and this is the last paragraph of it:
That, in the opinion of the minister, the construction of the pipe line by Interprovincial Pipe Line Company is in the national interests of Canada.
The committee, therefore, on the recommendation of the Minister of Trade and Commerce, advise that under the provisions of the Electricity and Fluid Exportation Act, a licence, in accordance with the form attached hereto, to construct a pipe line to connect at the border of Canada and the United States of America at or near Gretna, Manitoba, with a pipe line to be constructed in the United States, be granted to Interprovincial Pipe Line Company of Edmonton, Alberta, accordingly.
That was on the 13th day of September, 1949. Until that order in council passed, the board of transport commissioners would not make an order in the case at all. On the 15th day of September the board of transport commissioners made this order as reported in the speech made by the leader of the opposition at page 2325 of Hansard:
Upon hearing the application at the sittings of the board held in Ottawa, September 8 and 12, 1949, in the presence of counsel and representatives for the applicant, the province of Alberta, the Department of Trade and Commerce, the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, the city of Port Arthur and the board of trade of Fort William . . .
It is ordered that leave be, and it is hereby granted to the Interprovincial Pipe Line Company to construct a pipe line for the transportation of oil from a point in the vicinity of the city of Regina, in the province of Saskatchewan, to a point in the vicinity of the village of Gretna, in the province of Manitoba; the said pipe line to be constructed and completed on or before October 31, 1951.
Be it noted by those who believe that parliament and the government have no authority in this matter that that order was made two days after the order in council which I read just a moment ago was passed. In the face of those facts, in a similar circumstance, let us no longer quibble as to where the authority in this matter lies.
Another argument made by the supporters of the bill-and I think it was made by the Prime Minister when he spoke, but when the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra questioned him later he agreed that the point was not just exactly as he made it-is that the board of transport commissioners can decide in all circumstances the route the pipe line should follow. But leaving aside the point that I have already made, namely, that

the board of transport commissioners can move only after the governor in council has moved first, may I say that the board of transport commissioners is limited in its decision to the route in the application made to it and in the plans which accompany such application. I suppose it could, in its wisdom, decline to grant an order for the construction of a pipe line over any route whatsoever. I do not know; but I would be of the opinion that if this parliament passes a bill that gives authority to this company to build a pipe line either through Canada or through the United States, the board of transport commissioners will consider that, parliament being indifferent as to the route the pipe line should follow, it could authorize the laying of the pipe line on the route, whatever it may be, that the company making the application lays before it. In my opinion that is a logical conclusion. Let me repeat it. If we members of parliament are unconcerned as to which route the pipe line should follow, if we do not care whether Canada should be served after the United States cities are served, or that Canada should be served before United States cities [DOT] are served; if we are unconcerned in the matter and refuse to make a decision one way or another, the board of transport commissioners is justified in giving an order endorsing the particular route that is laid before it by the company making the application.
Anyone who has read the report of the proceedings of the committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines must be struck by the fact that, in so far as the companies making application having information in regard to the different routes are concerned, the great bulk of their information is concerning routes through United States territory. There is hardly any information at all in regard to routes through Canadian territory.
Let me quote briefly from the proceedings for Friday, April 28, where the hon. member for Calgary West (Mr. Smith) was questioning Mr. William C. Gilman:
Q. You have made no examination of the all-Canadian route. You do not know whether a line can be built between Hope and Princeton or not, do you?
A. No.
Q. Why are you giving us figures in millions per year to the lower mainland in British Columbia when you have nothing to base it on at all?
A. It is just an engineering guess of the cost of construction.
But, remember, the application is placed before tihe board of transport commissioners, and the costs of the various routes are placed before the board. These costs will also be an "engineering guess." And the $17 million
Prairie Transmission Lines difference in cost between building a pipe line through Canadian territory and through American territory is also a guess. As the hon. member for Coast-Capilano said when speaking in this debate, they just took that amount out of the air. But let us remember that when they get a charter for a pipe line they have something far more important than anything that can be pulled out of the air. The questioning continued:
Q. What do you mean by an engineering guess?
A. Well, all estimates are guesses.
What do you think of an answer like that? -"all estimates are guesses." I do not care how wise and fine a citizen that man may be, my conclusion, is that he took the committee for a pack of fools. I presume he thought the members of parliament on the committee, sent here by the electors of Canada to represent them in parliament and to make their laws for them, were intelligent men. Yet he tells them that all estimates are guesses. A guess is something one says in this fashion: "I guess it is going to rain tomorrow" or "I guess it will not rain tomorrow." What do hon. members think of that sort of evidence as something to make a decision on?
Then the questioning continued:
Q. It is a pious hope because you like the southern route? A. No, we have no preference at all.
And then later on:
Q. I do not know how I missed you. a distinguished looking gentleman like you.
A. I did not see you there either.
Q. The answer to that is I do not know why you should have. We will go on further: you have made no surveys whatever in the Yellowhead pass route?
A. No.
Q. So you do not know what the cost will be to take gas via that route, do you?
A. No.
Q. So you are talking about saving these hundreds of millions over a twenty-year period and you have no basis for comparison at all, have you, with the Yellowhead route?
A. I was not making a comparison with the Yellowhead route.
Then on the next page of evidence he was questioned by the hon. member for Vegre-ville (Mr. Decore):
Q. In connection with the Yellowhead route the only observation you made was when you went through by train?
A. That is right.
Q. Now, I just want you to answer this question. How fast was the train going when you were making those observations?
A. Oh, about twenty to twenty-five miles an hour.
There should have been one or two further questions, such as, "Was it during the day or during the night?" and "Were you awake, or were you asleep?" All these questions would be equally relevant, because

Prairie Transmission Lines the answers they received were just the answers that had to be given in a situation where those replying had no answers to give.
I could continue quoting questions and answers from these amazing proceedings, but it is not necessary. I have already quoted sufficient to show that the committee was nothing but a farce.
Another argument offered by supporters of these bills is that if we grant a charter to one company, and to one company only, we are creating a monopoly. The hon. member for Edmonton West was surprised that the Progressive Conservatives, who are in favour of free enterprise, should support a policy of monopoly, and that members of the C.C.F. who favour public ownership should also favour monopoly, or a course of action which would lead to monopoly.
Has anyone suggested that if we grant three charters three pipe lines will be built to the Pacific coast? Certainly no one has made that suggestion within my hearing. We know that of course no one has said any such thing, because there will be no business for three pipe lines to the Pacific coast. Consequently, no matter which company gets a charter to build a pipe line, it will have a monopoly. After all, a monopoly is not always necessarily a bad thing, and I think the hon. member for Edmonton West should know that. When the pipe line reaches Vancouver -should it reach there-I understand the distribution of gas will be carried out by the British Columbia Gas Company. A monopoly, if you like; but surely no one in this parliament is foolish enough to say that you could grant two charters fpr supplying Vancouver with gas. A monopoly is a bad thing when it is used to raise prices to the consumer through the elimination of competition. When you give one company a charter or a franchise to do a certain thing and keep control over what that company can charge, when you provide that they receive only an amount that is considered fair, reasonable for the service they give, that sort of monopoly is a good thing.
It is time we stopped talking nonsense. It is time we stopped trying to find alibis for following a course which reason indicates does not meet the requirements of the situation. I have heard it said on many occasions that Canada's resources are unlimited. They used to say years ago that the resources of the United States were unlimited. But the United States has consumed its resources to such an extent that it is looking more and more to Canada for raw materials such as ores and other raw materials to keep its


industries going. So far it has been the policy of this country to be content to sell our raw materials.
This committee should not be panicked by the specious argument that unless we grab this opportunity to sell our natural gas at once the United States will get its gas from some other source. They used to put up the same argument in 1910 when they were selling lots in Vancouver. When a real estate agent was trying to sell you a lot he would tell you he had a dozen buyers for it when he didn't have one. We are being told the same thing here. That is another alibi we should stop using. We have not unlimited resources.
The people of British Columbia are anxious that they should be given the first opportunity to use this resource. If there is more than we need there is no reason in the world why our American cousins cannot have it. These gas resources are ours and we should have the first opportunity to use them.
I had no idea when I rose to speak that I would speak at such length because I do not believe it is necessary to labour this question. I have said already that this parliament has an obligation to at least give an expression of opinion. If it cannot give a directive, it can give an expression of opinion that it wants this pipe line to serve Canadian needs first. Because this parliament has an opportunity to give an expression of opinion, because the first order must be passed by the executive of this parliament, that will be a directive as to what kind of order in council should be passed. Then the board of transport commissioners will have its cue. Hon. members from other parts of Canada have an obligation as members of this parliament to protect the interests of British Columbia.
When we have done that I am sure that the pipe line will be built through British Columbia, but if we let this bill through in its present form there is no assurance that the pipe line will be built through British Columbia.

I should like to deal with one or two resolutions passed by the fruit growers of British Columbia along these lines. They also have ideas on how to go about recapturing the world markets that we have already lost. This is one dealing with marketing missions:

Therefore be it resolved by the British Columbia Fruit Growers' Association, in 1950 annual convention,

I feel that Germany has either to remain a burden or to return to the family of nations. Personally I am opposed to rearming Germany, but I favour giving them all assistance to let them recover their agriculture. In other words, let them get on their feet again. One way is to supply them with the seeds they need, but that cannot be done because we are still technically at war with Germany. I understand that it may be a long time before a peace treaty is signed. Other trading nations have overcome this difficulty by effecting a treaty of commerce between themselves and Germany. I would ask the minister to get the proper department-I presume it is External Affairs-to endeavour to effect a treaty of commerce between Canada and Germany, and not wait for a peace treaty, and thereby give Germany a chance to recover on an agricultural basis so that she may meet her obligations to the rest of the world and particularly to Canada.

The information came from that department on December 5. In it they tell me:
The most recent information that we have received on the western German exchange situation as a whole is that they have been running behind to the extent of approximately $500 million a year, most of which deficit has been covered by grants from the United States. In these circumstances, we understand that they, like all recipients of ECA funds, have been under pressure to reduce and keep down their dollar expenditures. I suggest that our present trade, what little trade there is being done between Canada and Germany, is done with the grace of the United States of America, through the use of

I have one or two questions that I should like to ask the minister, but first of all I should like to make a few general remarks regarding the marketing of agricultural produce.
We have been told by the food and agriculture organization and other bodies that the population of the world today is expanding at a faster rate than our production of food. We are informed by the food and agriculture organization that the supplies of food per individual are today less than they were in 1939, and that even with expanded production it will continue to be less for the next six or seven years, and for a considerably longer period of time than that in so far as the Far East is concerned. Whether or not we benefit by that potential market will largely depend upon our own policy; that is, whether or not we adjust our international trade policies so that we are able to enter those markets.
During this session I think it has become quite evident that some at least of the ministers in the government lack confidence in our own international trade policy. I think that was shown quite clearly by the speech of the Minister of Fisheries when he suggested that in order to be able to increase our exports of certain products we should enter into barter agreements.

From time to time the Minister of Agriculture has expressed a certain degree of concern regarding our international trade. Today the farmers are being repeatedly told that they will have to make the price of their products competitive so as to be able to enter the markets of the world.
In order that farmers may make their prices competitive they will have to be in a position to reduce their costs of production. But unfortunately many of the farmers' costs are of an uncontrollable nature, and for the last few years those costs have been still increasing. Even as late as last fall the price of machinery took a sharp rise, freight rates went up and various other costs increased.
So I would say it is not so much a question of the farmers making the prices of their commodities competitive as it is of the secondary industries making the prices of their commodities competitive. Because, after all, if we want to sell farm products abroad we must enable nations to sell their products to us in order that they may obtain Canadian dollars with which to buy our produce; and in order to accomplish that tariffs will have to be kept down.
I think by now manufacturers in this country should be in the position to stand on their own feet. I was very much interested in a statement made by Professor Galbraith before the annual convention of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture. The report in the Manitoba Co-Operator of February 9, 1950, contains this:
If our manufacturers, both, in the United1 States and Canada, feel they must continue to have protection from European imports then they must candidly admit the consequences of their demands. Because of their need for protection, they are denying Europe dollars with which to buy agricultural products. Europe is thereby being denied access to the efficiently produced farm products of the western hemisphere because the manufacturers of the west, their vaunted) claims to efficiency notwithstanding, cannot stand the competition. The American and Canadian farmer is being asked to take the rap for them.
Again I stress the fact that instead of harping upon the suggestion that farmers must be prepared to make the prices of their products more competitive, we must realize that before that can be done the prices of products of secondary industries must also be made competitive. If the prices of manufactured goods fall, then the prices of agricultural products could also fall without any detrimental effects on the farmers. Because, after all, the farmer today is asking only for a price that bears a fair relationship to the prices of other commodities.
The government has set up machinery to provide support for the prices of agricultural products. This session that legislation was

amended so that it shall carry on indefinitely. It is well for people to remember that the farmers have already paid for that support by accepting for their commodities, ever since 1942, prices which were lower than world prices. If one considers the amount of money lost as a result of taking those lower prices, one will find that it is a very substantial sum. My suggestion is that it should be regarded as a reserve established for the purpose of maintaining fair prices in the future. I would say that the main concern of farmers today is the fear that prices will not be maintained at a fair level in the future.
I agree with statements made from time to time by the Minister of Agriculture to the effect that our chief market is the Canadian market. Also I believe we can all agree that even today the Canadian market is not developed to its full capacity. It is my view that the government should give careful consideration to adapting in some form the Brannan plan, which is gaining more and more support in the United States. I mention this especially in view of the fact that we are constantly faced with the danger of surpluses of certain commodities in this country.
For instance, we have had a butter surplus. I think when a surplus occurs the government should be prepared to introduce a policy somewhat along the lines of the Brannan plan under which those surplus commodities can be sold to the consumers^ of Canada at a reduced price. To put it another way, we cannot afford to allow the fear of a surplus to reduce our production. No one could suggest that such a policy could be justified in a world where many people face the danger of mass starvation.
I understand when the Minister of Agriculture was out west he recommended a reduction in wheat acreage to the extent of three million acres, and that the farmers increase their production of coarse grains and grasses. But when the Minister of Trade and Commerce spoke in the house on the wheat resolution he stressed the fact that we are having greater difficulty now in selling our farm produce. He visualized a certain amount of difficulty in selling our farm produce, other than Wheat, in the future. In so far as wheat was concerned he pointed out that he did not expect any difficulty in selling it because it is the best wheat in the world and our price is competitive.
I ask this question: If wheat is the one agricultural product we can sell readily, and if the Minister of Trade and Commerce feels there will be no difficulty in selling wheat in the future, is it really wise to reduce our wheat production and to increase the

production of other commodities which may not foe sold so easily? After all, if we extend the production of coarse grains and grasses it is 'almost certain to result in increased production of dairy products and hogs.
I believe the farmers are 'concerned about the sale of dairy products. We have heard a good deal about it in the last year, and there seems to be some uncertainty as to the future of the hog market. From the point of view of sound agriculture I would agree with the Minister of Agriculture one hundred per cent that it is in the interests of agriculture to reduce our acreage of wheat and to have more grasses if for no other reason than to restore the humus to the soil, and to prevent soil drifting. It is time we adopted some form of crop rotation. But from the point of view of whether or not we can sell our produce, it seems to me it is better to produce a commodity we can sell readily, when we have already been told by the Minister of Trade and Commerce, as I have already pointed out, that there will be no difficulty in selling wheat because it is the best in the world and our price is competitive.
Therefore when the minister speaks I would ask him to tell us what he considers the prospects are in regard to the sale of hogs in the future. What does he expect the hog market to be? Does he feel that farmers should go ahead and expand hog production-because I believe that is taking place now in western Canada. I know in the part of the country from which I come hog production is expanding. Can they continue that expansion with a reasonable degree of safety? Can they also expand their production of dairy products? If the minister is not able to give that assurance, then does he not feel it might be safer for them to maintain the present level of wheat production? Because, even if wheat does become a surplus commodity, it is much easier to store wheat than to hold hogs, once they reach the weight of two hundred pounds.

While we have butter we can adjust it as we think it ought to be adjusted. On this occasion we thought a downward adjustment of 5 cents ought to be made. I assume that over the years ahead of us in all probability for a time adjustments will be in a downward direction, but if the policy and plan continues over a term of years eventually we will come to a time when the adjustment may be down one year and just as likely be up a similar amount the next year. We may go down one cent or two cents one year and be up one cent or two cents the next year. One will balance against the other.
That is the plan which is in operation, and if we never get below 20 million pounds of butter we do not need to be worrying about it. If we never get above 20 million pounds we do not need to be worrying about it very much. The only time when you need to worry about being below that figure is around Christmas. Then one certainly should have about 40 million pounds of butter if you are going to take care of that market and see to it that nobody walks in and makes the consumer pay a price he never should pay. We ran into a difficulty which we did not expect to meet, and we have had a little experience which may suggest improvement. You will recall that for last year we set the end of what might be called the dairy year to correspond with the end of the financial year. That is not the natural end of the dairy year. The natural end of the dairy year is the last day of April, and the first day of May over a long period of years has been the first day of the new dairy year. We worked last year on the financial year in order to make it more convenient for those who were financing. When we came down to within a week or two of the end of that time we announced we were going to continue it for another month. A lot of people across the country who were running stores and taking more or less of a chance in connection with the matter, this being the first year of the operation, began to wonder whether they were going to be required to take the two cent, three cent, or five cent loss that people were talking about. Therefore they cut down their stocks in their stores so that they would not be loaded up at the end of the time and have to take a loss.
When it became apparent that we were going to take care of the adjustment, then most of them had their stocks provided in the ordinary way from their usual wholesalers without any great difficulty. I found, however, that a great many of the smaller stores around the country did not get stocks.

When they were not getting stocks the really live agents of those who were putting out oleomargarine put that product on their counters. In country areas throughout the dominion during the latter part of last season a great many farmers who were accustomed to using butter on their own farms were using oleomargarine. It is all very well to criticize it, and I do criticize it; but at the same time I realize it was the first experiment in the new plan and that people were likely to do things which they probably will not do a second time. Therefore with that experience we are hopeful that when we reach the end of another season there will be no great difficulty.
I say that in order to get out of the minds of those in this house who are thinking in terms of surpluses the idea that there is any surplus of butter that ought to scare anybody away from continuing to make it. Over all the years that I have had' anything to do with agriculture we have just made the amount of butter that we have been able to consume in this country, and we should go on aiming to do that. If we put enough of our enthusiasm and ability into the marketing of butter in this country I do not think we would need to be talking so much about oleomargarine, and by the very fact that we are talking about it more or less advertise its sale all over the country. Butter is the best food that is put on the market in Canada, and in accordance with food values it is the cheapest in these days of high food prices. That being the case, I do not see any reason why we should be worrying about any surpluses harming us in that direction.
Turning to cheese, it is a dairy product that has to be sold largely outside Canada. We have 17 million pounds, or we had a few days ago. I should not have said that we have 19 million pounds of butter. The last time I looked at the figures we had about 17 million pounds. At the beginning of the dairy year we had about 17 million pounds of cheese. The people of Canada eat close to 60 million pounds of cheese. We have 17 million pounds and the trade has 17 million which makes about 34 million, and we eat almost double that. We are requisitioning cheese to send to Great Britain. She has undertaken to take approximately 85 million pounds. We have been asked by the producers of cheese to requisition it until we fill the British contract, and that is what we are doing. Remember that the year before last we only produced 96 million pounds, and last year I think we produced about 114 million pounds. Since our production has been hovering around 100 million pounds a year, and if we are going to send 85 million to

Great Britain, and we only have 34 million in storage, there is not going to be any great difficulty in, marketing any amount of cheese which seems to be in sight during the year ahead.
In other words, what we ought to be doing in the house and elsewhere is telling the farmer to continue to produce as he has been producing and as he thinks he ought to produce. There has not been up to the present, and there is not likely to be ini the immediate future, any great difficulty in selling. We can sell all our butter on the Canadian market if our production continues at the level it has been. We sell most of our cheese in the British market. If there is any danger at all at the present time in the figures which I have just given you, it is that we may run ourselves a little short on the Canadian market, although we are not going to be in any great difficulty at the end of the season if our production continues as at present seems probable.
Therefore in so far as cattle and dairy products are concerned I think we should be going right ahead with production. I do not know of anywhere that the farmer can make more than he can by going ahead and producing beef cattle at the present time, and at the moment returns are very good from dairy products as well.
As to hogs, I think eastern farmers will continue producing them. I think it was the director of livestock in Ontario, Mr. Watson, who said at our conference last December that Ontario farmers depend for 60 per cent of their income upon dairy products and hogs. He went on to say they just could not stay on their farms without producing dairy products and hogs. I think every Ontario farmer realizes that. So long as that is the condition there is no need to worry about their production being cut very much. They keep their production at about the same level all the time. They did so in wartime, before the war, and are still doing so. In western Canada hog production rises when we find a shortage in the United' States or somewhere else which makes it possible for us to market great numbers outside our own country. Then hog production goes down when we find any excuse for letting it because we like to produce grain in western Canada a little more than we like to feed hogs. If we can find any really good excuse for cutting down on hog production we cut down and we stay down until we have reason to feed hogs again. I am not worrying about that side of it. At the moment all I am worrying about is that the cattle on our farms in western Canada are not in as great numbers as I would like to see.

The question before the committee seems to be when summer fallow is not summer fallow, but I would like to refer to the question of butter and hogs, which the minister was talking about a few moments ago. You know, the minister is an amazingly ingenious dialectician. For the first time tonight he brought forward the proposition that the floor price was put under butter to protect the consumers. The dairymen have been under the impression ever since this floor price was put in that it was done to protect them, to make sure the price of butter did not fall below 58 cents, which would make it impossible for them to produce, at any rate according to their own claim.
In addition to the dairymen I think up to this moment every member of this house was under that impression. We voted money, to the extent of some $200 million all told, as a sort of revolving fund which the minister could make use of to put floor prices under agricultural products. Not long ago he rose in his place in this chamber and said he had taken a certain amount of money out of that fund to put a floor price under butter. Certainly there was no question in our minds but that this support price was for the purpose of protecting the dairy farmers; but, as I say, the minister has now confided to us for the first time that it was not for that purpose at all but to protect the consumers. When the consumers read about this in the newspapers tomorrow I am sure they will laugh and laugh; but it is going to be a very derisive laugh. It will be very difficult to convince the consumers-

-that the minister has put this floor price under butter for their protection. He went on to say there was a

surplus of only twenty million pounds; in fact he said it was not a surplus but only twenty million pounds in hand. The hon. member for Greenwood suggests that it is just working capital, and hardly enough of that, so there is no need to worry about it at all. A little later on the minister said that during past years we have made in Canada just the amount of butter we could consume. That is more or less correct, of course; but I would point out to the minister that during those periods we were not consuming any margarine. I have not the figures at the moment, but if he will look them up I am sure he will see there has been a constant increase in the production and sale of margarine every month since it came on the market.
There is no use trying to delude the people of Canada or members of this house into believing that the sale of margarine is not going to reduce the sale of butter. Now that we are in the position of having twenty million pounds of butter on hand at the end of what you might call the storage period, when new production is starting and we are going to be building up our supplies of butter again, a year from now we probably will still have that twenty million pounds on hand, unless it is sold outside the country or used for industrial purposes or consumed in some other way. I do not think there is any other answer but that this twenty million pounds of butter is not going to be eaten as long as the relative prices of butter and margarine remain anything like they are at the present time.
In addition to this twenty million pounds, which in my opinion is an amount the minister is stuck with, we will say, and which he is going to have extreme difficulty in getting rid of anywhere, I should like to know how much of this butter which was taken over has already been sold abroad at cut-rate prices. I know that a certain amount has been sold to Germany. I do not know where else it has been sold, but certainly some has been sold- abroad at prices considerably less than the going price. We therefore now find ourselves, Mr. Chairman, in the ridiculous situation in which the minister is using this agricultural floor support price money to protect the consumer of butter so that he will have to pay for it more than the Germans or other people abroad have to pay for it. Of course the dairy farmer thinks he is being protected by it too, but that is an error, I guess.
I should like to know just where we are going in this matter. Certainly it does not make good sense. It seems to me that, instead of trying to persuade the committee

and the country that there is not a surplus of butter at the price at which butter stands at the present time, the minister should admit what the situation actually is, namely, that as long as margarine is being sold at the price at which it is being sold-some twenty cents or some figure in that neighbourhood below the price of butter-it means that we have not at home the market that we used to have, and that some other means must be taken of disposing of this butter. Otherwise the farmers must be persuaded to put their milk into some other form of production.
While I am on my feet, I should just like to comment on the minister's statement about hogs. It happens to be a subject I know something about. He said that hog production was quite satisfactory in the eastern part of Canada and he saw no reason why it would decline. In the west it has declined considerably, but he was not worrying about that. He did not think the farmers would go out of hogs any further than they had done-that is what I gathered from his remarks-and they were better to put their efforts into beef. With the present relative prices of beef and hogs, there is no question about the fact that a man is much better to be raising beef. There is no argument on that at all. I think the minister will admit that one of the main factors that discourage the farmer from growing hogs is the hog barley ratio, which means the price of coarse grains in relation to the price of hogs. In the last issue of this livestock and meat trade report put out by the minister's department, I notice that for the week ended April 29-which was the last one on record -the-hog barley ratio at Winnipeg was 14-1. The long-time average is 17-4. The figure of 14-1 is the lowest point it has been at for some considerable time.
I would suggest to the minister that that is one of the reasons why a great many people -and they are already doing so, as far as that goes-will get out of the hog business. People are not prepared to put in the labour which is considerable in raising hogs, when the relationship between the price of hogs and the price of coarse grain is so unsatisfactory as it is at the present time. I think the minister is deluding himself and is attempting to delude others if he has any idea that people are going to increase or even anything like maintain the present hog production in Canada as long as coarse grains are so expensive in relation to the price of hogs.

I make no apology, Mr. Chairman, for taking a few minutes of the time of the committee to bring to your attention and that of the minister some of the problems of my constituency.

Supply-Agriculture
Before proceeding with these few comments on the matters I wish to deal with, I think I can correctly say to the minister that, so far as my constituents are concerned, the fruit farmers are glad they have received some financial assistance from the dominion government towards the cost of the 1949 crop. The vegetable producers, I would say, are highly indignant over the unannounced' removal of the import restric-' tions on vegetables, and the poultry producers are just plain mad at the mangling they have had in the last three or four months.
I think it is generally admitted throughout the country thqt the minister has wide knowledge of his department and that he is thoroughly conversant with and interested in agriculture; but I think his strict adherence to the principles of the Manchester school of Liberalism prevents him from facing squarely certain of the marketing questions that are facing this country and the world today.
This evening I want to deal briefly with the question of land conservation, the use and conservation of water, and the proper use or utilization of land for agricultural purposes. I want to make a few brief remarks about the marketing problems faced by the producers, by British Columbia and by my own constituency. Then I want to bring to the attention of the minister and of the committee certain problems that affect my own constituents and certain suggestions that they have asked me to make as an indication of the remedies they think might be given effect to.
I am not one who believes that our production problems, our marketing problems, or any of these problems, can be solved in some easy and quick way. I realize that if we are going to work our way through these difficult times and find a democratic and satisfactory solution to these problems, it is going to mean co-operation between governments and co-operation on all levels of those interested in solving these problems for the common good.
I want to say a few words tonight on soil and water conservation, and on land use as related to agriculture, because I believe that [DOT] with millions hungry in the world, with thousands unemployed in Canada at this time, and with possibly thousands continuing to be unemployed at certain periods, we cannot continue to waste our land and water resources, to waste our opportunities for producing that necessary food and to waste the opportunity of providing labour if we aim to plan to give that labour something to do.

I wish therefore this evening to deal with a suggested national policy of soil and water conservation and land use which has been drafted by the Agricultural Institute of Canada and which I understand was presented to the minister about a year ago. I understand that this policy was the result of several years' work. It is the result of, shall I say, a combination of idealism, intelligence, brains, science, knowledge and hard work. I am a member of the organization myself; and personally, I am of the opinion that this worth-while professional organization of scientific agriculturalists in Canada have not performed a more useful service than they have in presenting this policy to the Minister of Agriculture and to the nation. Because I have been interested throughout my life in land and water conservation, in conservation measures of all types, I do not apologize in any degree for bringing this matter to the attention of the committee at this time.
Just to give one illustration, Mr. Chairman, of the great need of some national policy in this respect, I want to deal briefly with a situation that has existed in my own constituency for over 45 years. I know the great need on the prairies, in the maritimes and in other places; I know the general need, but in a few moments I can give an illustration of deplorable neglect and inaction because of the lack of a policy of the type suggested by the Agricultural Institute of Canada.
There is in my constituency a very beautiful valley known as Lardo valley, which is about 30 miles in length on the northeast of the Kootenay lakes. In that valley will be found some 500 million feet of uncut timber, matured. It should be cut now. It should have been cut many years ago. It is virgin timber. There will also be found some 10,000 to 15,000 acres of first-class land. There are abundant water supplies. There is everything in that valley to build up a stable agricultural and forestry industry over a long period of time, and to provide home sites and farms for hundreds of people. But today, because of a lack of a national policy on land and water use, and the co-operation required between federal and provincial governments, this great opportunity remains neglected; remains neglected, Mr. Chairman, while we have thousands of young Canadians who are anxious to secure farm sites and opportunities to farm under somewhat pioneer conditions at reasonable rates; young men who have not the $10,000, $15,000 or $20,000 required to establish themselves on an improved farm close to larger centres of population, but who

are seeking an opportunity to establish themselves at a low cost and to develop a farm with little capital, but as the result of hard work and sticking with it.
In this valley we have this land, we have the timber, we have the water, and yet for years we have had federal government experts go in there and look the situation over for another department of government, not the Department of Agriculture. They reported the fertility was there, the water and the timber were there, but nothing could be done. They would not recommend settlement because 12 miles of a road had to be built to give communication from that valley to the outside world. Provincial government inspectors have done the same thing, and have reported that 12 miles of road were required, and there were no services. There was no small hospital; there were none of these services required to establish a small community.
This has gone on, as I say, for 45 years, because there is no co-operation between the provincial and federal governments and no interdepartmental co-operation. If we are to develop great assets like that in this country we must have a policy that provides for co-operation between federal and provincial governments and between departments.
Not only is co-operation necessary between governments to develop a project such as that, but it would require the co-operation of the Department of Agriculture and the Department of Public Works, to look after the navigation and the draining of rivers. It would require the co-operation of the Department of National Health and Welfare and the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys. But we lack that departmental cooperation-and I find, Mr. Chairman, so often that governments become extremely departmentalized. In this instance a question arose of removing a log jam from a river at a relatively small expense, so that boats could tow booms down the Duncan river. It would have meant an expenditure of around $4,000. I happened to mention to one public works official that this lowering of the dam would not only provide for navigation but would also lower the river at high water, and drain some 3,000 to 4,000 acres of beautiful black land in the Meadow Creek area. I was immediately told that I must not suggest that; that the Department of Public Works had nothing to do with draining land. If it was going to do that it could not be considered; that it must be strictly for navigation. And yet one little 55946-157
Supply-Agriculture
operation, and a little expansion of one operation, would have meant the draining, not of
3.000	or 4,000 acres only, but of 10,000 or
12.000	acres.
I give that, Mr. Chairman, as an illustration of the lack of departmental co-operation.
I am not blaming the heads of departments;
I am not blaming the officials; it just results from the lack of a national policy of soil and water conservation to make the best use of our land and water for agricultural and other developments.
Now, Mr. Chairman, I am going to place this policy on the record. I am going to read it because I think it is a document which is well worth bringing to the attention of this committee and well worth bringing to the attention of the Canadian people. The policy reads as follows:
The Agricultural Institute of Canada therefore urges:
(a)	that the dominion Department of Agriculture recommend to the government of Canada the immediate establishment of a national policy of soil and water conservation and land use for Canada, and that the government make provision for the necessary legislation;
(b)	that under the act there be appointed a dominion co-ordinator of soil and water conservation and land use;
(c)	that a national council on soil and water conservation and land use be established on a joint dominion and provincial basis, with sufficient powers to implement programs according to the need across Canada;
(d)	that having regard for the variable nature of soil conservation, reclamation, andi land and water utilization, procedure, and practices across Canada, and inasmuch as the land resources of Canada are for the most part vested in the provinces, the custodianship and conservation of our land and water resources available for agricultural purposes be the responsibility of the department of agriculture in the province concerned;
(e)	that the provincial governments be asked to provide the legislation, administrative organization, and educational services necessary for the effective utilization, conservation and reclamation of soil and water resources and further that they be asked to design ways and means of encouraging cultural and land use practices which will maintain and enhance the productivity and usefulness of our soil and water resources;
(f)	that the provinces provide such legislation, aid and guidance to municipalities and farmers as will permit them to effectively perform their duties resulting from soil and water wastage and deterioration;
(g)	that under the provincial legislation there be established local autonomous committees to implement land use and soil and water conservation projects;
(h)	that the dominion and provincial governments inaugurate an immediate program for the training of personnel adequate to provide an advisory service to farmers, and
(i)	that in view of the immediate need for an advisory service to farmers, existing staff be trained and used to the fullest possible extent.

Supply-Agriculture
It is the opinion of the Agricultural Institute of Canada that under the above legislation and organization the necessary agreements between the dominion and the provinces can be implemented.
The above program is recommended by the Agricultural Institute of Canada to provide a broad national policy for the conservation of the land and water resources of our dominion.
I heartily agree with that policy, and it appeals to me in many respects. It does not ask the federal government to do everything or the provincial government to do everything. It means, if implemented, satisfactory co-operation between federal and provincial governments and farmers or, should I say, the rank and file concerned. I think it combines the opportunity for government direction and government guidance with self-help, local improvement and local interest.
That program has been presented to the Minister of Agriculture, and about 8,000 reprints have been sent to interested individuals and organizations throughout Canada. In a matter like this, which is a somewhat abstract question to many people who may not think deeply on these problems, problems which in many cases do not affect them directly because of the lives they lead, it takes time to build up public opinion in support. I know however from my acquaintance with large numbers of people in Canada, and my knowledge of a good many organizations and institutions, that there is a slowly growing interest in Canada at this time as a result of the efforts put forth in this proposed national policy by the Agricultural Institute of Canada, and that there is decided public opinion in favour of the establishment of such a policy.
This policy has been recommended by the Canadian Federation of Agriculture. Interest is being taken in it by universities and other educational institutions, by development organizations across Canada, by chambers of commerce, by labour organizations, by business organizations and so on. In fact, I have before me a list of twenty-nine major institutions, organizations or business concerns which are now taking a direct interest in the promotion, knowledge and understanding of the policy I have just read to the committee.
When the minister replies before his estimates are concluded I would ask him to tell the committee his opinion of this policy, and to state whether there is any possibility of the dominion government's accepting the recommendations and giving some effect to them in the immediate future.
I wish to deal briefly with world market surpluses. I shall be brief indeed because I support the remarks of the hon. member for Acadia, and I do not think it is necessary to repeat them, more than to underline what he said about the necessity for accepting the
[Mr. Herridge.l
policies advocated by the Canadian Federation of Agriculture and by the International Federation of Agricultural Producers with respect to the need for a world pool for the distribution of agricultural surpluses.
May I make a few brief comments with respect to the fruit industry of British Columbia. When I speak for the fruit growers I speak as one who has been interested for forty-five years, who has grubbed out stumps. So at this point I do not represent those farmers who ride on rubber-tired tractors and who use the big machinery with headlights, and all the rest of it. I represent the farmer who walks behind the walking plow, the farmer who uses the mattock, the shovel, the pickaxe, the axe, and other instruments of that kind. I represent the small farm hewn out of the forest.
But I do suggest that our fruit growers of British Columbia do urge that greater efforts be made by the government, particularly by the Department of Agriculture and the Department of Trade and Commerce, to develop the potentialities of the British market for our fruit. We believe those departments have underestimated the possibilities of that market. When we read of Australia making a deal less than a month ago for three million boxes of apples, and of apples being shipped from Italy and other countries, we realize that when we were told a year or two ago by a representative of the Department of Trade and Commerce that Great Britain would be nearly self-sufficient in apples, because of heavy plantings, we were not told the facts. I think that in this connection it would be proper for me to quote Sheridan when he said that the honourable gentlemen were using their memories as far as their wit was concerned, but their imaginations as far as their facts were concerned.
I do urge that every effort be made to explore the future possibilities of the United Kingdom market, knowing of the difficulties which are created by the exchange situation.
I wish to express my appreciation-and I am now referring to the United States market-of the work that has been done by the Canadian Horticultural Council and its sister organization in the United States in meeting together each year and coming to some sort of arrangement. I think the work of both organizations is welcomed and recognized by the government when they make a mutual arrangement with regard to the shipment of apples to the United States and possibly some importations into this country. They try to work out their marketing arrangements on a mutual basis. I think the method of working out quotas so far as possible, especially into an area where the need is

found, and back again where the need is found, will be the development of the future, rather than dependence upon tariffs and tariff restriction.
Our growers believe that, if we are to meet the situation which will face us at the end of this crop year, the government should now commence to plan to implement its price support policy, and to give some evidence of the formula it intends to use in respect of certain crops. I am of opinion that we will get a satisfactory solution for this question only if we have co-operation between all governments and producer organizations. I believe all will agree that farmers are not unreasonable; the average farmer seeks to make only a reasonable living. He is not expecting more than his share of the total production of society.
But I do suggest that the time is ripe for the government to commence to study its floor-price program rather than to take action when the need appears urgent as a result of the necessity to dispose of our crop. In this connection I should like to read a resolution adopted by the British Columbia Fruit Growers Association which has to do with the Canadian subsidy for export fruits. This resolution arose because of the fact that Canadian apple producers, tree fruit producers, are meeting exceptional competition from American producers because those American producers are receiving the export subsidies. The result was that this resolution was passed in January by the British Columbia Fruit Growers Association:
Whereas the offshore exports of fruit from the tree fruit area of British Columbia is of paramount importance to maintaining fair market conditions, and
Whereas it has become increasingly difficult to enter the offshore export market, due to the devaluation of currency, and
Whereas United States growers are able to enter these markets by means of a government subsidy on apples and pears shipped offshore,
Therefore be it resolved by the 1950 B.C. F.G.A. convention that the dominion government be requested to give serious consideration to the giving of a subsidy on offshore shipments of Canadian tree fruits.
I bring that to the attention of the minister because our organization is of the opinion that it may be necessary as a temporary move to consider subsidies for some offshore shipments under these very uncertain world marketing conditions.
I should like to make brief reference to the poultry industry. I feel sorry for the poultry industry because it is not organized in the same way as the beef and dairying people are, and particularly as these grain growers in front of me are. Because of that 55946-157J
Supply-Agriculture
they sometimes fail to make their voices heard with the government and with the trade as well as some other sections of agriculture do. Unfortunately they seem to be misunderstood by the consumers.
I urge that every consideration be given to the present position of the poultry industry and to the possibility of establishing satisfactory floor prices.
I think something should be done towards supplying feeds at reasonable prices. When I was home at Easter I had the opportunity to examine some feed wheat and feed barley and other grain which had been shipped in for poultry feeding purposes. I am of the opinion that the distribution of mill feeds for livestock and poultry is well worth the special attention of the Department of Agriculture. Some of the samples of wheat I examined were almost unfit for stock or poultry feed. I did not have the opportunity to get many samples, but I believe a high percentage of weeds and dust and so on would be found. I suggest that the minister have his department give particular consideration to this matter.
I am getting closer to home all the time and I have now landed in the Kootenays. I want to express the thanks of our people for the work of the officials of the department in connection with the little cherry disease. We think they are doing a good work and we realize the difficulties of the problem they are facing, but I have one criticism to make. Because of the interest of the cherry growers in the investigation it would be a good thing if the officials could keep the farm and fruit growers' organizations informed periodically of the progress being made in trying to find a solution to the little cherry disease problem.
I am not as pessimistic over this as some people are. When it first occurred many people threw up their hands and thought that was the end of the industry in the Kootenays. I think without question we produce the finest cherries in British Columbia. Personally I believe the disease is the result of soil unbalance caused by excessive irrigation, over-application of fertilizers and things of that sort. I am a great believer in barnyard manure and green crops in connection with the production of cherries. Our orchard practice of excessive irrigation and fertilization, especially nitrogenous fertilizers and leeching, has produced a soil unbalance that has affected the vitality of the tree.
I have knowledge of a tree which bore little cherries, that is cherries with less sugar content than normal, somewhat pointed in shape and lacking the normal colour, for two or three years, and then later on bore normal

Supply-Agriculture
fruit. I repeat that in my opinion this is the result of lack of vitality occasioned by soil unbalance.
Our organization, as well as those in the Okanagan, are greatly interested in the research being carried on by the department with respect to the use of cull apples and little cherries, and also the possibilities for making cider. I come from a farm family in England and we used to make excellent cider from Pippin apples. We make a considerable quantity of cider at home for our own consumption but we have never been able to make the same grade as we used to make in England. It may be because of the different apple varieties that are used, but I do urge that more research be carried on with respect to cider production.
I support the hon. member for Yale when he suggests that the Department of Agriculture should put out some counter-propaganda against that of the Department of National Health and Welfare which is so eulogistic about citrus fruit juices to the disparagement of the possible use of apple juice.
Before concluding I want to make a plea on behalf of our vegetable growers. There are a number of vegetable growers who supply the local markets in the interior of British Columbia. In the spring of last year they planted their celery, their leeks, their cabbages, their carrots, in fact their usual crops believing they had the protection of the import regulations. They had ample markets for their crops provided they had that protection. They are most indignant at the fact that the import regulations were suddenly raised after they had been induced to plant those crops because of the shortages that existed in the district.
I want to point out to the Minister of Agriculture, in the hope that he will use his influence with the Department of Finance, that there are root cellars full of cabbages, carrots, beets, turnips, leeks and other vegetables at a time when carloads of similar vegetables are being brought in from the United! States. Here is a case where the Department of National Health and Welfare could do something for the Canadian vegetable producer.
The consumer in the city believes that he must have fresh carrots and cabbages and lettuce from California. As a matter of fact, if you take one of these small bunches of carrots that you get at the present time and cut off the tops you will find what you are actually getting. Our people would be far better off if they would go out and buy good Canadian carrots that are now in root cellars waiting for a purchaser. The Department of National Health and Welfare could well

direct the attention of the Canadian consumer to the value of vegetables that are grown normally in order to counteract the drift of the consumer toward the use of quickly grown vegetables which all nutritionists say are not as nutritious as those grown in a normal way with the normal moisture and mineral content, vitamins and so on.
I do hope the minister will give some consideration to providing protection by some means for our vegetable growers. I am not suggesting a tariff, but I do suggest that the quota system is an excellent thing. So long as we have unsold vegetables in Canada let them be sold first. If our local supplies had been allowed to come on the market in the normal way they would have been exhausted earlier last winter. When they are exhausted then there should be an arrangement between vegetable growers' organizations here and in the United States to import sufficient to meet Canadian requirements. I think many of these things can be settled by mutual agreement and adjustment particularly if the growers concerned can meet face to face as they have in the horticultural industry.
In conclusion I suggest that the matters I have brought to the attention of the house can only be solved as a result of co-operation between federal and provincial governments, producers' organizations and farmers as individuals. In British Columbia we have an excellent producers' organization in the British Columbia federation of agriculture. In Tree Fruits Limited we have a marvellous marketing organization unequalled anywhere in the world, and I make that statement without fear of contradiction. It is efficiently operated. The organization is controlled by the rank and file, and it is democratic from its head to its toes. It is well run in every respect. I suggest that if the government is willing to bring together all these great forces of democracy, federal, provincial, local and individual, then in solving our agricultural problems we will also be doing something to solve the problems of democracy as a whole.

One or two questions have been asked which I think I should answer tonight because I and those who asked them may forget them before we come back to the agricultural estimates. The first speaker this afternoon made some suggestions as to travelling expenses and miscellaneous items. He said that some $190,000 odd in the agricultural estimates was for different items which he said were sundries, n.o.p. and contingencies. I think most of ours are not classified under any of those heads but rather are described by a different name from any

of the three which have been used. In every branch we have miscellaneous items. I presume that is the term to which my friend was referring. All I wish to say in reply this evening is that we will deal with each one of these miscellaneous items as we come to it, and will be in a position to give explanations as to the purpose for which the expenditures were made. Generally speaking the items are comparatively small or are ones that cannot be classified properly under any one of the other items in the branch, and they are all put in the miscellaneous item.
At the same time I might say that it is not a matter with which the officials of our department have a great deal to do. Those who have the responsibility of compiling the estimates put all items that they consider should be so classified under the different headings in the estimates, and those which they are not able to classify are put under miscellaneous. We have a complete explanation for every item in that category which we can give when we come to the different branches of the department, but at the moment I do not think I should go through all these items and select them. We will be prepared to make explanations as we go along.
As to travelling expenses, I note that the amount mentioned was $2,148,000. The item is fairly large but as the hon. member said at the time he mentioned it I doubt if there is any department where it is more necessary to have fairly high travelling expenses than the Department of Agriculture. Much of the work which is done has to be done in contact with farmers scattered widely over Canada, and if not directly with farmers then with organizations which are more or less localized across the country. For that reason considerable travelling expenses are involved. I should like to repeat what I said as to the other item, namely, that travelling expenses run through all the different branches of the department, and I think it will be much more beneficial to deal with them as we come to them under the different items. I think it will be better to explain them then rather than to attempt to give any general explanation at this time.
The last speaker referred to a report made by technical agriculturists throughout Canada. As everyone knows, technical agriculturists across Canada are largely officials of our department and the departments of the different provincial administrations from one end of Canada to the other. They also include professors of Canadian universities who are associated with the agricultural division of university work. These men and women are
S upply-A griculture
the ones who actually carry on the activities of the department. I have glanced rather hurriedly at the recommendation which they made. I have not had an opportunity to study it closely but I venture to say that their recommendation involves in large part pretty much what is being done in connection with agriculture in Canada.
1 remember when I came to Ottawa fifteen years ago one of the first conferences I attended was a conference called for the purpose of discussing the overlapping of activities in different federal departments with relation to different provincial departments. It was generally admitted by all those who attended the conference, which was a general one covering all departments, that there was as little overlapping in departments of agriculture across Canada as would be found in any other department of government. In other words, there was very little of it found in any particular place. Wherever it appears, to some people that there is overlapping it will usually be found on examination that 3 co-operative set-up has been established which makes it possible for our officials to do provincial work where it is better to have it done that way, and for provincial officials to do our work where it is better to have it done that way.
The system we follow in connection with grading inspection, for example, is to appoint provincial officials as our officials where we require to use them, and the provinces, appoint our officials as provincial officials where they require to use them. There is every degree of co-operation that could possibly be brought about in that regard. We have joint plans throughout as to soil surveys, and work in co-operation with university staffs. We contribute toward that work, as do the provinces. We do a certain amount of the work here and a certain amount is done in the provinces but there is the most complete co-operation among those who are concerned with that particular kind of work.
The same thing is true as to research. While some of our research work is done by the national research council, by far the greater part of it is done ini agricultural schools and colleges, and universities that have an agricultural campus in addition to. the main university campus, as many of our universities now have. They are all working; together in the matter of agricultural research from one end of Canada to the other. Having said that, I agree with the suggestion that there should be much more of it. If we could get the funds I believe a great deal more research work could be carried on in all parts of Canada with beneficial results. As a matter of fact we have representations

from certain sections of Canada that not as much research work is being done there as somewhere else, and we are constantly being urged to speed up our research work in certain areas.
The same thing might be said of reclamation work. From time to time we have discussed the possibility of bringing down legislation which would spread P.F.R.A., for example, over the whole of western Canada in order to take care of reclamation work. We have had suggestions that other legislation should be brought down covering eastern Canada which would be more or less an enlargement of the legislation we now have dealing with the reclamation of the marshlands in the extreme east. At one time we had hoped to bring down legislation this session covering both those activities, but I am sorry to have to say that because of the delays in connection with the discussion of financial matters as between the dominion and the provinces, in all probability we will delay bringing down that legislation until after the conference that is to be held.
Let me say at once that this does not mean there is likely to be very much delay in the work that can be planned within the next year. In connection with P.F.R.A., for example, we have a sufficient number of dug-outs applied for in the area described as the Palliser triangle to take care of all the work we could do in probably two seasons if we applied ourselves entirely to work of that kind. So there is no need for delay in anything that requires to be done, because of the lack of legislation this year. Again, probably all the money we would be able to obtain for that sort of work during the coming season is already required in connection with the reclamation work being carried on in the marshlands of the maritime provinces and other assistance we give here and there along the St. Lawrence, the great lakes and elsewhere. Much of that work is being carried on under special votes, so I think perhaps we are doing fairly well in that direction.
One matter was touched upon by two speakers from British Columbia that rather stirs my sympathies. I remember going to British Columbia many years ago and attending one of those summer picnics they have at the Summerland farm. For the first time I had the opportunity to drink apple juice, apart from the hard cider we used to drink down in Ontario in the earlier days. I came back an advocate of the drinking of apple juice in this country. The war came on shortly after that and we had no market for our apples, so we put on a strong advertising campaign to promote the consumption of apple juice. My particular part was that no

matter where I went, east or west, when I went into a restaurant or hotel I asked for apple juice. Now I can get apple juice everywhere, except in one line of restaurants in Canada. At first I thought it must be a line of American restaurants-

speechtext: I do serve it sometimes; but there is one line of restaurants well established in this city and in most cities across Canada where I cannot get it. I go there less and less often because I require apple juice three times a day; but when I ask for it the waitresses tell me they just cannot get their management to provide apple juice. One of these restaurants is only about two blocks from where we are meeting tonight; another is in one of the prominent hotels of this city. I go right on asking for apple juice, however; and I think if everyone who went there, particularly those from British Columbia, would do the same thing in all probability we would get that management to provide apple juice. After all, one way to get these things used in Canada is to ask for them. When I see persons who come from apple-growing areas walk into a restaurant, particularly for breakfast, and ask for orange juice I rather resent it when they get up in this house and suggest that we are not doing enough to help them.

speechtext: Then I take that back as far as my hon. friend is concerned. Many others do ask for orange juice constantly instead of asking for apple juice, but I can assure my hon. friend I never do. I ask for apple juice every morning for breakfast and I usually get it, because I do not go to that restaurant when I want breakfast. The other evening I was there after the theatre and asked for apple juice. They did not have any, so I said there were about two thousand people around here with whom I had some influence, and I was going to suggest to them one of these mornings that they begin to boycott that place until they serve apple juice. I do not think it does any harm to talk that way occasionally; perhaps if we all did it we could get those restaurants to serve apple juice. I agree with my hon. friend that it is a delightful drink, even were it not npurish-ing.
